utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. One moment only. [Interpretation] Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. I will begin with the submissions for the Defence of Mr. Mrksic in relation to Rule 98 bis of the Statute of this Tribunal. Bearing in mind the norms of this Tribunal, as well as standards applied by this Trial Chamber and other Trial Chambers in previous cases, and also bearing in mind that we come from a legal system where there is no concept of acquittal, I will try to limit my submissions under Rule 98 bis to what I believe to be appropriate in view of the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. Before I begin with the submission of our arguments under this rule, prior to that I would like to raise some issues as Defence counsel which I believe to be justified in view of the modified procedure applied before this Tribunal. The purpose of the application of this rule, Rule 98 bis, is to enable the Trial Chamber, after the end of Prosecution case, to analyse the evidence led until that moment and to establish to which extent the Prosecution managed to prove the allegations in their indictment concerning the criminal responsibility of the accused. The purpose of this is to contribute to the procedural economy and to avoid evidence by Defence that is not necessarily needed. I believe that this rule is limited to a situation where the Prosecutor failed to produce such evidence based on which a Trial Chamber could conclude that no reasonable trier of facts would consider such evidence to be sufficient to prove -- or, rather, to base beyond reasonable doubt a conviction on them. It seems to me that the standard is that Rule 98 bis needs to be applied only in such cases where the evidence led by the Prosecution is such that even when viewed in the gravest light they wouldn't be capable of supporting a conviction. We need to bear in mind the need for judicial economy and speedy proceedings, and perhaps it wouldn't be too strong to say that a Trial Chamber is entitled to go a step further, because there is no jury, so it is the Trial Chamber which decides on conviction, and this in a sense is a usurpation of the role of a jury in the common-law system. The Trial Chamber will have to assess evidence at the end of the trial, and I think that they will not overstep their authorities if, at this stage, when analysing evidence led by the Prosecution on its own as well as in the context of all of the evidence presented during the Prosecution case, they conclude that in relation to certain counts of the indictment the Prosecution failed to prove the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt. The duty to prove the allegations contained in the indictment rests with the Prosecution, and the Prosecution must comply with this obligation in this stage of the proceedings, because during the Defence case the guilt of the accused is not going to be proven if it wasn't proven beyond reasonable doubt during the Prosecution case. In this case we have a situation where the Prosecution did not call a large number of witnesses here to testify, and these witnesses were participants in the event. Rather, on some occasions they relied on hearsay evidence, which is a peculiarity of the Rules of this Tribunal. Naturally, the Prosecution decides how they want to present their case. It is their prerogative. But we think that the Trial Chamber should assess whether the Prosecution could have proven beyond reasonable doubt already in this stage of the proceedings certain allegations from the indictment, so that the Defence would not need to lead evidence concerning those allegations which were not proven sufficiently in accordance with the standards contained in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. I think that this view is supported by the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, which allows the Prosecutor to put forward broad charges which in turn makes the proceedings much more complex. Thus, a broader application of Rule 98 bis was proposed, and it goes beyond the jurisprudence of national courts. It is just a mechanism that is used in order to ensure the efficiency of the proceedings. Thus, the Defence of Mr. Mrksic will turn to those counts of the indictment which we believe were not sufficiently proven during the Prosecution case. When it comes to individual criminal responsibility under Article 7(1) of the Statute of this Tribunal, the indictment in Counts 4 to 12, the Defence of Mr. Mrksic believes that during the Prosecution case the Prosecution failed to support these counts with evidence based on which this Trial Chamber could establish, beyond reasonable doubt, that the accused Mile Mrksic was one of the participants in the joint criminal enterprise, nor could the Trial Chamber establish that he planned, instigated, aided or abetted or committed any of the acts in relation to that as stated in the indictment. The Prosecution didn't lead any evidence to prove that the accused Mile Mrksic was a participant of joint criminal enterprise who, in agreement -- who acted in agreement with other participants of this JCE as stated in Count 7 of this indictment. The purpose of his action was not persecution of Croats and other non-Serbs, as listed in the indictment, and the Prosecution did not provide sufficient evidence to support this allegation. When it comes to Count 9 of the indictment, the Defence believes that the Prosecution failed to prove, under (b), that he knew that on the 18th of November, 1991, in Zagreb an agreement had been reached between the JNA and the Croatian authorities on evacuation of patients from the Vukovar Hospital. They didn't adduce a single piece of evidence to support this. Neither does it stem from the statements of witness Dr. Vesna Bosanac who gave evidence here before this Tribunal. Under (c) of this same count, Count 9, in view of the Defence, the Prosecution didn't prove, didn't adduce evidence based on which the Trial Chamber could establish, beyond reasonable doubt, that the accused Mrksic ordered that the detainees from the Vukovar Hospital be surrendered to other Serb forces, as is stated in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I just intervene, Mr. Domazet. We believe that you're referring to Article 9 and Article 7, or paragraph 9 and paragraph 7 of the indictment, rather than to Count 9 and Count 7. Is that correct? Paragraph 9 is the paragraph which sets out (a), (b), (c) and (d), particularly against your client, and I think what you're speaking about, is referring to those.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I used the word "count" instead of the word "paragraph." So yes, I would like to correct myself. A minute ago I spoke of paragraph 7 of the indictment, and now I'm referring to paragraph 9 of the indictment. So when it comes to paragraph 9(c), and the order for the issuance of which the accused Mrksic is charged, I believe that no evidence was led by the Prosecution to support this allegation. As for 9 D, where the accused Mrksic is charged with -- I'm now quoting from the indictment: "After becoming aware that the criminal acts charged in this indictment had been completed, took steps to hide and conceal these crimes." The Defence believes that there is no evidence to establish that the accused Mrksic learned of this, and then took these steps, and if so when. The Prosecution failed to prove it during their case. They also didn't prove what measures precisely the accused Mrksic took in order to hide and conceal these crimes. Now, as for paragraph 20 of the indictment, even though it may not be of vital importance, the Defence believes that the accused cannot be considered to be bound by law and regulations as set out in the Law on All People's Defence and the Law on Service in the Armed Forces of the SFRY from 1988. In view of the Defence, these regulations on the application of the international laws of war on the armed forces of the SFRY pertain only to the international conflicts, which was not the case in our trial. As for basic facts listed in paragraphs 24 to 27 of the indictment, the statement of facts, the Defence of Mr. Mrksic believes that the Prosecution did not adduce evidence to show, I'm quoting now that: "The non-Serbs were subjected to a brutal occupation regime, and that ultimately almost entirely non-Serb population in the occupied area was killed or driven out." As well as that members of the JNA, upon taking control of Vukovar, which, in the indictment is described as an occupation, I'm quoting that: "They, upon doing that, killed another several hundred non-Serbs." In view of the Defence, there is no evidence to support that this was done by the members of the JNA. Additionally, it is our view that the Prosecution did not support with evidence facts stated in paragraph 30 of the indictment. I'm quoting: "On 19 November 1991, Mile Mrksic was ordered by the JNA command to evacuate Vukovar Hospital pursuant to the agreement reached in Zagreb on the 18th of November, 1991." This was already discussed previously; namely, the position of the Defence, that the Prosecution failed to prove that Mile Mrksic was informed at all about the Zagreb agreement. Similarly, there is no evidence to support what is stated in this paragraph; namely, that he had received an order by some JNA command. We did not see any such order, nor were we able to infer that, based on the evidence led. In paragraph 37 of the indictment where there are allegations about how the detainees were led from the hangar in the direction of Grabovo, when using the terms "Serb forces comprised of JNA," the Prosecution in relation to that did not lead evidence based on which the Trial Chamber could establish beyond reasonable doubt that this was, in fact, so. In view of the Defence, there is no evidence to support that the soldiers of the JNA took part in driving away and physically exterminating detainees. Even though it is true that Witness P-022 participated in this, based on his own evidence here, that is not sufficient proof of the participation of the JNA soldiers, because, among other things, even if this Trial Chamber is to believe the evidence given by this witness, he was present there outside -- or, rather, without any orders issued by his superiors. He didn't have a prescribed JNA uniform that had been issued to him and that he had worn prior to that. He didn't have the JNA-issued weapon; rather, he had some kind of a hunting rifle. It is clear that his alleged participation in this has nothing to do with involvement of the JNA soldiers. It is our view that the Prosecution failed to prove paragraph 37, where they state that the JNA soldiers were among those Serb forces, as the Prosecution calls them, who led away and killed detainees. The possible involvement of P-022 can in no way be considered to be tantamount to JNA involvement or indeed to prove that the JNA soldiers were involved in the killing of at least 264 Croats and other non-Serbs as set out in paragraph 38. Speaking of this figure, the Defence believes it cannot be accepted as proven by the OTP that at least 264 Croats and other non-Serbs were killed. The figure could be at the very most about 200 persons, mostly Croats but also others, not just non-Serbs, but rather also Serbs. Paragraph 38 of the indictment contains an allegation by the OTP. The allegation is as follows: The bodies of the victims were buried in a mass grave by using a bulldozer. The Defence respectfully submits that this does not follow from any evidence that has been adduced. None of the evidence so far indicates that this type of machinery, anything resembling a bulldozer, was used. We do believe that the Prosecution have failed in proving this. Paragraph 39 of the indictment claims that on the morning of the 21st of November, in Vukovar, at Nova Ulica 81, Radic, Vujanovic and others, but certainly not Mrksic, not including Mrksic, who was himself never in Vukovar on those days, the paragraph claims that these people discussed the massacre that had occurred at Ovcara. The OTP here claims that Mrksic knew about this conversation and that based on this knowledge he could and should have taken steps to punish the perpetrators. The Defence has already pointed out our belief that there is nothing to indicate that Mrksic took any measures to destroy evidence or conceal the crime. We do believe, therefore, that the OTP have failed to prove Mrksic's knowledge of this conversation, if indeed such a conversation ever took place. He could not have known about this, and there is no evidence to show that he could. Speaking about paragraph 41 of the indictment, the Defence believes that the Prosecutor has failed to prove persecution on political, racial or religious grounds. The maximum figure would be 200, and certainly not 264, as stated in the indictment, which would include all the different ethnic groups, including Serbs, although the predominant group among those were Croats; that is beyond doubt. Further, the Defence believes that the Prosecution have failed to prove that sexual violence was perpetrated against at least one woman. This is in paragraph 41(b). Paragraph 44 is repetition of something that the Mrksic Defence has already challenged on several occasions. There is the allegation that at least 264 Croats and other non-Serbs were taken in groups to a location southeast of the Ovcara farm where Serb forces comprised of JNA, TO -- or rather, comprised of, among others, the JNA, executed them. These facts have been challenged on numerous occasions as facts simply not proven by the OTP. As for the allegation in this paragraph that the names of victims are set out in the annex attached to this indictment, one thing we must bear in mind is that during this trial it has been proven that a total of 200 bodies was exhumed from the Ovcara mass grave. Two of the identified bodies are, in fact, not on the list attached to the indictment. Also, in the course of this trial it has been established that 14 persons from that list were buried at the new cemetery in Vukovar and not at Ovcara. Speaking about paragraph 46 of the indictment, the Defence must repeat something that we have already said. It has not been proven that only Croats and non-Serbs were victims, nor has it been proven that there were about 300 of them as stated in this paragraph. Likewise, the Prosecutor has led no evidence to prove - and now I'm talking about paragraph 41(b) - that at least one female person was subjected to sexual assault. Your Honours, this is the position of the accused General Mrksic's defence under Rule 98 bis under the Rules of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And good morning to you, Your Honours. As for the proposed application of Rule 98 bis, the Defence is aware of the positions of this Chamber in relation to the ruling that is to follow pursuant to Rule 98 bis. We know that it is not the time today to evaluate the guilt of the accused under the counts of the indictment or the totality of evidence that has so far been adduced. However, we must say that the credibility of certain witnesses, their weaknesses and strengths, as well as the contradictory nature of some evidence is also not something that I am now here to point out. However, something that Mr. Domazet has already said is that the Chamber, based on evidence judged in the most favourable or gravest possible light, depending on the view-point, can sometimes acquit, even based on that one single piece of evidence. However, there is a very important theory here in favour of the fact that if there is even a shred of evidence, but a relevant shred of evidence, viewed on its own terms and yet found so wanting, so unconvincing, a reasonable trier of fact can never lend it the same credence or weight as the best and strongest evidence, and therefore such evidence cannot be used as a basis for acquittal. The Radic Defence will use or employ the same system as in the previous case. We shall challenge the responsibility of Radic under 7(1) and 7(3). We shall also be addressing the individual paragraphs. It won't be until the very end of my argument that I will address the counts and specific charges brought against Miroslav Radic for the crimes alleged in the indictment. As for Miroslav Radic's individual criminal responsibility, the Prosecutor would needed to have proven either direct perpetration of the crimes stated in the indictment or the existence of a joint criminal enterprise that the accused was part of. It is this concept of joint criminal enterprise that is mentioned in 7(1) as pertaining to Radic's individual responsibility. There must be justification in purely cumulative terms for proving this. There must be solid proof of the existence of such a plan in addition to the physical perpetrators alleged by the OTP. The OTP does not say that these three accused were directly involved in the perpetration of any crime at all. However, the Prosecutor would then needed to prove the mens rea of these three accused, something that they shared with the physical perpetrators, the mens rea of the accused as suggested by the OTP. The most important intent, the most important common intent must be backed by such convincing evidence that even when such evidence is viewed in the most unfavourable light there can be no acquittal. I will not be speaking about aiding and abetting, because this comes down to an element of volition, and this is something that is essential in relation to all three accused. I will be addressing this specific issue through the individual counts. If we go from paragraph 4 to paragraph 12, we will realise the following. Paragraph 5 of the indictment claims that the purpose of this joint criminal enterprise was the persecution of Croats, specifically those who were present in the Vukovar Hospital and were then taken to Ovcara, where the crimes of murder, extermination, torture were committed, as well as other inhumane actions. This is under Article 3 and Article 5 of the Statute. What I find myself obliged to tell the Trial Chamber now is that Radic was a small-time commander of a small-time company within the 1st Guards Motorised Brigade. The Prosecution have proved nothing beyond that. They have succeeded in proving that he acted in accordance with the rules governing the services in the armed forces. He took part in these operations, house-to-house, street-to-street operations, and this is why I'm calling the overall nature of his enterprise small-time. He was acting as a military officer. He had certain orders, and he restrained from doing anything else but carrying out those limited orders. And the element of volition required for persecutions was certainly not there. In relation to paragraph 5, there is no solid evidence adduced by the OTP to show that Radic was involved in the evacuation of the hospital. Alleging his presence there merely to corroborate the indictment can only be described as unconvincing evidence, and no reasonable trier of fact could ever convict based on this one single piece of evidence. Paragraph 6 of the indictment addresses the objective of the joint criminal enterprise. Obviously a joint criminal enterprise requires the presence of several people who take part in it. The Prosecutor cites this as one of the proofs that the joint criminal enterprise existed. However, what is essential is a common plan, a plan shared by all these co-conspirators, which the Prosecutor has done nothing at all to prove, especially as concerns my client's involvement. The beginning of this enterprise or plan is alleged to have occurred in Seselj's alleged speech, which is a political pamphlet to all practical intents, but that cannot be taken as an incipient plan. I will address all the counts of the indictment individually to explain this. If by describing Seselj's visit between the 13th and the 15th of November, 1991 as the beginning of a joint criminal plan, and provided the Prosecutor has been successful in proving the date at all, we know that no agreement was reached on that occasion between Mrksic, Sljivancanin, Radic, Stanko Vujanovic, Miroljub Vujovic, or anyone else present there. The Prosecutor has never managed to prove that some of the accused were there at all at this critical time. Further, the Prosecutor did not prove that a plan was designed so that this speech could be taken as the beginning of a plan or an enterprise. By this criminal enterprise crimes were committed against persons, as the Prosecutor claims, who were brought from the Vukovar Hospital to Ovcara. This would probably imply that as soon as now there was an agreement on the evacuation which was generally known, or, rather, that persons belonging to certain groups would at this point in time be taken to Ovcara for an execution. It is also beyond reasonable doubt that the Prosecutor proved the evacuation of the Mitnica group, but it is against this very background that we should realise that the Prosecution has failed to prove that following such a common agreement and a joint criminal plan that all Serbs should be killed and driven out of Vukovar. Quite the contrary, in fact. This is a positive example showing how military enemies can be evacuated in keeping with the rules without the presence of a broader plan at this point in time. The mens rea of the accused Radic would imply that the Prosecutor has thus proven the existence of this joint plan or common intent [as interpreted]. Now, under this assumption that there was no common plan, no joint criminal enterprise, then we would need to assume that it was other perpetrators who committed these crimes, these serious criminal offences. This may have been the result of a common plan or joint criminal enterprise by some other people. But how could then Radic have been part of this plan and how could he be held responsible? By way of conclusion, Radic was not involved in any sort of joint criminal enterprise. The Prosecutor has failed to show that on this particular occasion when Seselj spoke Radic in any way took part in this. I can quote evidence by witnesses to show this. Radic did not speak about any sort of plan or enterprise, nor did the Prosecutor show that Radic reacted in any way at all to this alleged beginning of a joint criminal enterprise. I base this on Prosecution witnesses P-002, P-018 and P-022. Needless to say, there is not a single witness statement to prove otherwise. I would like the Chamber to view these circumstances in the light suggested by OTP witnesses themselves. "Not a single Ustasha must leave Vukovar alive." This is something that a politician may have stated, but this could also imply that there was a military victory involved. We had evidence adduced here, Exhibit 567, which was a newspaper article demonstrating that Seselj was fighting against fascists and that he did not believe that all Croats were Ustashas. So by promoting, putting forward such ideas, the Prosecutor presents a false premise, and I don't think that this false premise requires us to deal with it seriously, either at this stage or any other stage of the proceedings. Paragraph 7 of the indictment, I think I've already mentioned this in passing, the Prosecutor failed to prove that Radic had any kind of an agreement with Mrksic, Sljivancanin, TO members and volunteers. Paragraph 8, which under (b) says that Stanko's house was the command post. Once again, I would point out that layman even referred to this location as an operations headquarters, command headquarters, or command for major military operations in Vukovar. All of this is of declarative nature aimed at supporting only verbally this indictment. However, we know that certain witnesses, especially witness Trifunovic, were quite firm in their statement that a command post can be established only within large, high-level formations starting from battalion and up. So this is not just a matter of military organisation, no. This was stated in Prosecution case by Prosecution witnesses in these very terms. Paragraph 10(a) is quite interesting in my view, especially in relation to my client, the accused Radic, because it is stated here that he had effective control over Serb forces, those who were responsible for crimes committed against non-Serbs taken from the Vukovar Hospital. The Prosecution did not prove here that Radic had de jure or de facto effective control on the one hand; and on the other hand, under (b), subparagraph (b), it is stated that there were 400 non-Serbs involved. In another place they speak of 300 non-Serbs, which means that the Prosecution, first of all, wasn't clear as to the number of people involved. That's one. And two is that Radic did not have either de facto or de jure control. He certainly didn't [realtime transcript read in error "did"] have de jure control over Serb forces. I don't want to trouble the Chamber by describing who comes into this category. We are quite familiar with this. The Prosecution did not undermine the evidence presented by Defence; namely, that after the 14th of November, 1991 -- Your Honours, line 20 -- or, rather, page 20, line 12, it should say that he certainly didn't have de jure effective control. Thank you. What the Prosecutor did prove is that the crime was committed; however, Miroslav Radic, as I have said, after the 14th of November, in accordance with Exhibit 430, 431, didn't have de facto control either. I'm not going to go now into who had such control. This is something that the Prosecution should prove, even though it is apparent, based on the orders that were introduced into evidence here. If we were, however, to go into details, then we would say that the Prosecution didn't manage to successfully challenge the evidence that in Petrova Gora there was a commander of the 1st Assault Detachment, 1st Motorised Battalion, that it was a location where TO forces of Petrova Gora were stationed, as well as Leva Supoderica detachment. So even when that is taken into account, he has an inferred de facto effective control in addition to de jure control, and this was not challenged by the military experts of the Prosecutor, including General Pringle. This means that in this portion the Prosecution failed to adduce evidence and convince the Trial Chamber that after this date, even if everything else is ignored, that after this date Radic had any effective control over these forces. Exhibits 374 and 418, which a bit ago I linked with the de facto control of the commander of Petrova Gora settlement, is something that further supports these facts. In paragraph 10 they speak of personal participation in the removal and selection of about 400 non-Serbs from Vukovar Hospital early in the morning on the 20th of November, 1991. This is paragraph 10(b). I think that in this instance the Prosecutor offered in support of their allegation only one single witness, P-030. Even if we were to accept that it was true that he had heard the name, everything else in this evidence is simply completely unconvincing. He spoke of a person who was up to 40 years old, of quite dark tan, 180 to 185 centimetres tall, or rather --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 175, 180 centimetres tall.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We know that my client was much younger at that stage, and he doesn't have dark complexion and his height is 192 centimetres. As for the uniform and his head-ware, this is something that is quite standard within the JNA. Military expert Pringle didn't support this thesis either when giving evidence. However, even if we were to assess this evidence in the most favourable light, it would still fall into the category of unconvincing evidence that I mentioned in the beginning of my address. Even if viewed in the most favourable light, no conviction could be handed down based on this evidence. It remains unclear to the Defence, and I believe that in the end it would be borne by the facts that a lot of valuable time, valuable for the accused, for the Trial Chamber and for all other participants in these proceedings, was lost while proving this allegation that Radic personally participated in the removal and selection. The Prosecution has two witnesses at least one of whom claims, "I'm the one, not Miroslav Radic, I'm the one who personally participated in the removal and selection, and I'm the one who had a list of 15 people who took out of a bus 15 people who were later set free." I think that clear evidence is needed here, not some semi-evidence which is used to trap the accused. By applying the principle of justice this cannot be upheld, and this must be the most important principle as frequently stated by this Trial Chamber. We believe that in this instance the Prosecutor failed to prove this. It is quite clear that it is the military police who is in charge of frisking, taking people to buses, and possibly selecting them. My client, who was a commander of a company, is not entitled to issue orders, nor did the Prosecution prove that he did this. As for the command responsibility under Article 7(3) of the Statute, it is clear that it is necessary for the superior/subordinate relationship to exist, also for the knowledge of the superior to exist. The Prosecution should have proven that he had the position of superior in relation to these forces and that he had the actual knowledge that a crime was going to be committed. Not a single legally relevant piece of evidence was offered in support of this allegation. As for him knowing or having reason to know, that is yet another standard which was not achieved, because the Prosecution offered meager evidence concerning the government of SAO Western Srem, Baranja and so on. Radic didn't know about the sessions of the cabinet government, their decisions. Miroslav Radic did not go to Ovcara. This was not even suggested by the Prosecution. As for the tasks concerning the securing of the hospital, removal and selection of detainees, he could not have been involved in this, thus he, as somebody who does not have effective control over, quote unquote, Serb forces, he could not be held responsible under Article 7(3) of the Statute in this portion of the indictment either. Thus, he could not have taken reasonable and necessary steps. Perhaps there were some other officers who could have done that, which is something that the Prosecution could have proven. These officers were at a higher level than an inconsequential company commander such as Miroslav Radic. Now, as for subparagraph (c), where it says that he took no steps -- or, rather, that he took steps to hide and conceal these crimes, I think that this is clear, based on witness evidence, but the Prosecution didn't prove that he took any steps to hide or conceal the crime. That's one. Two, is if we know to whom these forces belonged on the 14th through the 18th, and if we know what status they had on the 20th and 21st and following that, then, once again, it is clear that no valid evidence was offered by the Prosecution in relation to this either. As for paragraph 13, I think that simply saying precisely for these reasons the Prosecution has no evidence to support this. Paragraph 16 is quite interesting in terms of legal interpretation. In the second portion of paragraph 16 it is stated this: "During the operations against Vukovar and its aftermath, Miroljub Vujovic and Stanko Vujanovic ... were each subordinate to Miroslav Radic." First, during the operations we heard here that Stanko Vujanovic was in the direction of the company of Captain Bojkovski. The Prosecution didn't prove at all that he was under the command of Miroslav Radic. And to try to mask this by saying that the house of Stanko Vujanovic's father is proof enough that he was there is simply not valid. Stanko Vujanovic didn't sleep in his father's house during Vukovar operations. He slept somewhere else. Witness P-022, transcript 50-77/20, and then once again we come to this witness who says under whose control Stanko was, this is transcript page 4957/17. Other witnesses gave evidence concerning this, and the Prosecution failed to provide clear evidence concerning this allegation. Even the experts were quite reserved, had reservations about this allegation that Stanko Vujanovic was under Miroslav Radic's command. After Vukovar was liberated, after the 18th of November, we can see this in paragraph 16, the second portion of it, there was not a single piece of evidence to show that they were either de jure or de facto under the effective control of Miroslav Radic. Paragraph 19. Once again, we didn't hear any evidence offered by the Prosecution that would convince us that Miroslav Radic was notified that the detainees were threatened, that harm was caused to them, and three, that their subordinates were about to commit criminal acts. Not only was he not notified, but he also did not have effective control over these people at that point in time. This goes along with what I was saying previously. Paragraph 20. In this paragraph, we only challenge, and this is something that the Prosecution didn't prove, that -- or, rather, we are saying that they were not duty-bound to comply with the regulations on the application of the International Laws of War in the Armed Forces of the SFRY from 1988. In these regulations, the declaration of war is not mentioned; rather, an imminent threat of war. Due to these formal legal reasons, this regulation may not be invoked as a basis for responsibility of these accused. If we were now to turn to paragraph 23, which discusses crimes against humanity, we would see that it is stated at length here that all of these acts were part of a wide-spread and systematic attack against the Croatian and other non-Serb population. I don't think this is the place or the time to discuss the status of the civilian population. In the Blaskic case, it was explained that the persons who were in the Vukovar Hospital would not have enjoyed that status, simply because they failed to meet the six requirements under the Geneva Conventions. In relation to some of the accused, Radic principally, the Prosecutor has not proven that these acts were the result of a joint criminal enterprise and plan. I will again remind the Trial Chamber that Radic was a mere company commander. He was in no position to get in touch with any high-ranking officers in the area. As for paragraph 23, the Defence asserts that the Prosecutor has failed to prove this, to prove any allegations from these paragraphs. All these could have been were random and individual incidents, at best. Paragraph 26 mentions meetings at Captain Radic's headquarters, the objective of these meetings was to plan military operations in Vukovar. The OTP have not proved, even if we take into account these verbal explanations by laymen, that this was a headquarters at all. It could not have been a headquarters by any stretch of the imagination. This is not where the liberation of Vukovar was planned. The only command where plans were made was the command post of the commander of the 1st Motorised Battalion. Commanders came there pursuant to their orders and pursuant to their plans, the TO commanders who were deployed along the same operations axis. Paragraph 27, and obviously when the Prosecutor says "persecutions," they mean the evacuation. I don't think the evacuation can be used in this sense. Your Honours, Count 1 of the indictment, persecutions, is definitely not something that the OTP have been successful in proving, and this is what Miroslav Radic is charged with. Seselj's arrival did not give rise to any sort of joint criminal enterprise, as I've explained. That would have led to these crimes being committed. P-094 [as interpreted], page 4194/12, 434; P-022, the transcripts, 4985/25. I see that the page numbers are not being recorded, but probably it's a good idea not to go to these page numbers, because there is no time and this is something that I have spoken a great deal about. Witnesses P-024, P-022 and P-030. Again, there is a reference here to paragraph 33 of the indictment, the selection of detainees. Again, there is no evidence to show that Radic was involved in the selection process. If we take into account the unconvincing evidence of P-030, we can easily conclude that he never said more than search, searching and frisking. There was no selection, as such. Paragraph 34 is something that remains entirely unproven by the OTP; namely, that Major Sljivancanin ordered Radic to take a list containing 15 names and take those people off the bus. The Prosecutor has not proven paragraph 39; namely, that Radic, Vujanovic and others discussed the massacre that had occurred at Ovcara during the preceding night. Witness P-002, which is probably the witness invoked by the OTP here, says that he did talk to a number of people and later asked Vujanovic about these circumstances. Later he does say at some point during the evening, but then there is a different statement where he says several days later he claims that he spoke to Radic which in response to unconclusive action and unclear answers asked by the witness he said that they had not discussed the massacre at Ovcara the previous night. The OTP never managed to prove that the word "massacre" or "crimes" or "Ovcara" were used in this conversation. Even their own witness could not corroborate this. I see that I have two minutes left, which means that I will try to abbreviate this. The Trial Chamber has been following the Prosecutor's evidence. I don't believe they have been successful in proving any of the counts between 1 and 8, the counts that my client, Mr. Radic, is charged with. Regardless of what I said at the beginning of my address to the Trial Chamber, when I said what a 98 bis ruling should be, I still do not believe that I have now misused this rule. I believe that a sufficient number of conditions and circumstances have been accumulated over the course of the OTP case for the Chamber to acquit. After all, my client is here charged with counts that have no foundation in evidence or reality. This is all that I wish to tell the Trial Chamber today. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Borovic. We will have the first morning break now, resuming at 20 past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I will first make a general introduction to indicate how our Defence team sees the situation we are facing under these 98 bis proceedings. The Defence teams in this trial hail from a legal system that contains no provisions that are related to the general nature of Rule 98 bis, the chief reason probably being that our original legal system is founded on the principle of objective truth and not on the principle of proving guilt beyond reasonable doubt. In our own system, the role of the court is far more active in both gathering evidence and deciding on the presentation of evidence. The role of the parties to the proceedings is less pronounced than here, as a result. That is why, under our 98 bis rule proceedings, we shall be trying to present our arguments, both in terms of our experience and our professional standards, more in relation to the jurisprudence of this Tribunal and its established practice, as well as all the legal principles that it invokes. It is not easy to refrain from evaluating evidence as a whole or to draw the key distinction between the strengths and weaknesses of various testimonies, its contradictions and discrepancies. The Chamber will not be considering that now, nor will it be making abstract evaluations on specific evidence, whether it may perhaps be found wanting to warrant a possibility of conviction. The point in this trial at which we are now is about the fundamental role of the Court to accurately analyse the proceedings so far, in order to contribute to judicial economy and make it possible for the Defence to avoid unnecessary evidence in our case. We fully support the spirit of this article, although we do not think that the Prosecutor should be allowed to use broad and vague accusations throughout the trial. The latter, the fact that the Trial Chambers accept that the Prosecutor conveys his whole case on a vague indictment throughout, is the opposite of judicial economy. From the very beginning of the trial, and especially after the end of the OTP case, what this leaves the Defence with is an obligation to challenge many allegations of the indictment that are simply groundless allegations. In most of the cases tried before this Tribunal in the final ruling an accused, as a rule, is acquitted on a limited number of counts. Normally the Prosecutor drops the charges or there is a 98 bis ruling. Such a decision, a timely one, would greatly expedite our Defence case and reduce the length of the trial. This Defence team believes that it is up to the Chamber to channel any charges that are too vague, leading only to a trial that is too lengthy. I believe that even in our national -- in those national jurisdictions in which the standard known as no case to answer is applied if trials were as unwieldy, with such a massive amount of evidence, and even facing a clear pressure to expedite proceedings, Rule 98 bis provisions would be made better use of. The Defence must indicate another fact that seems to follow from the OTP case. At this juncture, the Chamber can consider and analyse what it was that the Prosecutor so forcefully announced at the beginning of the trial and what in turn was led in evidence during their case. They decided not to call some of their key witnesses. I use the word "key" here merely to indicate how many times the statements of these witnesses were invoked in their pre-trial brief. The Prosecutor showed that their approach to presenting evidence is not at all aimed at informing the Trial Chamber about all the facts in the OTP's possession and everything that they had previously announced. To put it in the simplest possible terms, the OTP does not wish to contribute to establishing the truth. They now leave the Defence in a situation that is not mandated by the Statute or the Rules. By shifting the onus on the Defence, the Prosecutor leaves the Defence in a position that it should never be expected or asked to face. At this point in time, the Chamber, certainly because it is not familiar with the statements or evidence of these potential witnesses and probably will never be, because the rule does not allow for that, the Chamber cannot assess how well the Prosecutor has met the requirements that he set out at the beginning. One thing that is certain is that the onus of producing evidence should not be on the Defence but rather on the OTP. I will now move on to my specific proposals, and my proposals are in relation to forms of individual criminal responsibility under Rule 98 bis. I am going to assess if there is any evidence to the charges contained in the indictment. First I will say something about the responsibility under Article 7(1) contained in the indictment. The Prosecution did not provide evidence based on which a reasonable trier of fact could conclude that Sljivancanin in any way participated in the joint criminal enterprise, as is stated in paragraphs 4 to 7 of the indictment. If we begin from the thesis that the goal of that enterprise is as the Prosecution defined in paragraph 5 of the indictment and paragraph 259 of their pre-trial brief, then there is simply no evidence to support that Sljivancanin had any ties to that plan, if it ever existed. In accordance with the appeals judgement in the Tadic case, paragraph 227, in relation to actus reus, there is no evidence to indicate that the third requirement, namely the participation of the accused in the very commission of the crime which, in accordance with paragraph 4 of the indictment, Sljivancanin is not charged with at all. Nor is there evidence to show that Sljivancanin aided and abetted or contributed in any way to the implementation of the common plan. The Prosecutor didn't adduce evidence to show that Sljivancanin had the requisite mens rea which was established as a standard in that same judgement, the appeals judgement in Tadic case, paragraph 228, both for the first category as well as the third category, or third type of JCE. Specifically speaking, in relation to the first type of JCE, that he had the requisite intent to commit a particular crime. In order to rule pursuant to 92 bis motions, the Trial Chamber has to establish, that all of the members of the JCE were involved in the commission of the crime, specifically that Sljivancanin, I'm going now to quote from the ruling in the Brdjanin case under 98 bis, paragraph 28, namely that he intended -- "[Previous translation continues] ... [In English] ... common plan and voluntarily participated in furthering the crimes in question." [Interpretation] I will read it once again. Paragraph 28. "It is required that the Chamber establish that the accused -- "[Previous translation continues] ... [In English] ... the result of common plan and voluntarily participated in furthering the crimes in question." [Interpretation] I see that it's not in the transcript. It is not running along. Maybe I should read it in B/C/S, but I wanted to use the original text. I'll read it once again. I apologise to the interpreter. I should have announced that it was going to be in English. "[In English] Intended the result of common plan and voluntarily participated in furthering the crimes in question." [Interpretation] Now I will go back to my native language. Now, in relation to the third category or third type of the joint criminal enterprise, the Prosecution didn't provide a single piece of evidence to prove the alleged intention of Sljivancanin to participate in and to implement the criminal activity of a group or to contribute to the joint criminal enterprise or to the commission of the crime by the group defined in paragraph 7 of the indictment. The Prosecution didn't prove that Sljivancanin was aware of any sort of a plan, and thus he was not able to foresee that acts listed in paragraph 2 to 8 of the indictment were a foreseeable consequence of the commission of this common plan. Based on the above, the Prosecutor didn't provide any evidence based on which a trier of fact could accept the allegations from the indictment mentioned in paragraph 12. The Prosecutor didn't prove, didn't lead any evidence based on which any trier of fact could establish that the acts listed in paragraph 11, subparagraph (a) to (i), are in any way related with the criminal plan and implementation of the objective or joint criminal enterprise. The Prosecutor especially didn't prove that Sljivancanin knew that on the 18th of November an agreement was reached in Zagreb between the JNA and Croatian authorities. This is subparagraph (b) in paragraph 11. I will now follow on what my colleague Borovic said, that it is not clear to us to this day why, and based on what, in paragraph 11(c) the Prosecutor mentions the number of 400 non-Serbs, whereas in paragraph 33 that number is about 300. We believe that no evidence -- there is no evidence to support that about 400 persons were led out of the Vukovar Hospital on the 20th of November in the morning. Given the above-mentioned requirements, Sljivancanin didn't know, nor did he have reason to know that these persons would be persecuted and killed. There is not a single piece of evidence required by this standard in Rule 98 bis to show that Sljivancanin participated in the joint criminal enterprise by committing acts listed in paragraph 11(g). In addition, there is not a single piece of evidence to show that Sljivancanin took measures to hide or conceal these crimes as stated in paragraph 11(i). In relation to individual forms of responsibility under Article 7(1) of the Statute, the Prosecution in their pre-trial brief spoke of the orders in paragraph 277 of their pre-trial brief, and then in paragraph 282 and 285 they spoke of aiding and abetting. Thus, I will put forward the position of the Defence concerning these issues. As for the ordering, the Prosecution failed to prove that Sljivancanin ordered that any crime listed in the indictment be committed. There is no evidence to show that he had the requisite mens rea for ordering. They needed to lead evidence which would show that he intended for this unlawful act to be committed and that he was also aware that there was a substantial likelihood that crimes were committed, as is established in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal; namely, in the appeals judgement in the Blaskic case, paragraphs 41 and 42. Finally, the special circumstances surrounding the position of Mr. Sljivancanin within the chain of command, and we will speak of this further when we get to the command responsibility, do not support the claim that Sljivancanin had any sort of authority, including an unformal authority over the persons which committed the crime physically, authority needed in order to issue an order. Now I would say something concerning aiding and abetting under the criminal responsibility pursuant to Article 7(1). In their pre-trial brief, in paragraph 285, the Prosecution lists the acts which constitute aiding and abetting of Mr. Sljivancanin, and they said that this would be proven in the Prosecution case. Further, they say that he had ordered that people be transferred from the hospital to the barracks, that he prevented the international observers from attending all segments of the evacuation, that he oversaw the detention of persons in the barracks, that he permitted people to be transferred from the barracks to Ovcara, and that he allowed the security organs of the guards brigade and the 80th Motorised Brigade to transfer the detainees to other forces knowing that they would be subjected to further persecution and killing. The actus reus needed for aider and abetter as defined by the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, in appeals judgement in Tadic case, paragraph 229, where a distinction is made between these forms of criminal responsibility and those within the joint criminal enterprise. I also refer to Vasiljevic appeals judgement case, paragraph 102 and Aleksovski appeals judgement case, paragraph 164. I always feel a bit weird where I had to point out to the Trial Chamber certain paragraphs in certain judgements. I think that you are the last people to whom this needs to be pointed out because you're quite familiar with this. In the appeals judgement in Krnojelac case, paragraph 51, in relation to mens rea, the court needs to establish that the accused, as aider and abetter, was aware that through his acts he provided significant contribution to the crimes committed by the principal perpetrator. He has to be aware of basic elements of the crime committed ultimately by the principal perpetrator. In relation to specific charges that the Prosecutor described concerning this form of liability, the Prosecutor didn't prove at all that Sljivancanin was aware of the acts of main perpetrators, principal perpetrators, and the intention of those who committed the crime of murder and persecution, nor was he aware that they would be committing these crimes. There is not a single piece of evidence based on which a reasonable trier of fact would be convinced that Sljivancanin was aware that by committing -- by participating in the evacuation of the hospital he would demonstrate that he was aware of the acts committed by main perpetrators, principal perpetrators. Now I will say a few words about the command responsibility. In its decisions this Tribunal established clear criteria that are needed in order to come to the conclusion that the accused had a command post and that he, as a result of that, has command responsibility. These are the well-known requirements stated in the appeals judgement in the Celebic case, paragraph 186 to 198 and 266. One of the elements needed, I would even say a prerequisite for other two requirements, that the Prosecutor needs to prove, is that the perpetrator of crimes was subordinated to the accused. This is Celebic judgement, paragraph 303. Within the principle of singleness of command and subordination, which existed within the Yugoslav People's Army, and this was something that was frequently invoked by the experts of the Prosecution, and also this was mentioned in many documents and regulations, it is clear that even in the temporary chain of command, there must be just one single superior, and the subordinates, those who committed crimes, were under his command within the command and control sense. The Prosecutor is not stating that the effective control of Sljivancanin in the evacuation itself is something that existed outside of the chain of command, no. They're saying that he had a command post or command function based on a temporary chain of command that was allegedly assigned to him. The Prosecutor didn't provide any evidence to show that this chain of command, which existed during the evacuation of the hospital, and which was defined in paragraph 17 of the indictment, functioned within the relationship that existed between Sljivancanin as a superior, on the one hand, and direct perpetrators of the crime, on the other hand, who were his subordinates. Many pieces of evidence indicate that this chain of command functioned within a different context at all, and it existed between other people, which the Prosecutor didn't want nor could they de jure link or put in the subordinate relationship in relation to Sljivancanin. The Prosecutor explains the responsibility of Sljivancanin in paragraph 17. They acknowledge that Sljivancanin did not have a de jure command authority in the Guards Motorised Brigade, as stated in paragraph 299 of their pre-trial brief. Rather, they paint this fictitious picture that this temporary command function was given to him by Mr. Mrksic. This is stated in paragraph 30 of the indictment and paragraph 36 of the pre-trial brief. In proving this factual claim, in their pre-trial brief the Prosecution invokes three documents. This is footnote 57 of the pre-trial brief. Two of these documents became exhibits in this case. This is Exhibit 425 and Exhibit 368. The third document is still pending on the 65 ter list. It is marked 573. All of these documents are reports of the Operations Group South, and the dates are 15th of November for one document, and two documents are dated the 22nd of November -- or 21st of November, 1991. Correction for the interpreters: Line 7, page 38, two documents are dated the 21st of November. These are the exhibits that I mentioned that you can check. With all due respect for the tactic used by Prosecution in order to interpret the documents, it remains completely unclear to the Defence what is it that the Prosecutor found in these documents that would be related to the alleged command position of Sljivancanin. Not a single piece of evidence led during the trial could convince a reasonable trier of fact that this claim of Prosecution is correct. De jure a command function is a formal function, and there must be strong incontrovertible evidence to prove this. What is beyond doubt is that in terms of his function, in terms of his position, Sljivancanin was in no position to exercise command. As far as we could tell, the OTP have offered no such proof during their case. OTP expert witness, General Pringle, in his report and in the evidence he gave before the Trial Chamber deduces the command role of Sljivancanin based on a witness statement mentioning him allegedly giving orders in the hospital during the frisking. This is testimony by persons who were in no way at all familiar with the chain of command in the Guards Motorised Brigade or in OG South. The only thing that such evidence can be used for, now that the OTP case has been concluded and we have a 98 bis ruling session, the only thing they can suggest is a possible existence of a de facto command function over members of the military police, and no more than that. As for the possibility that de facto command responsibility existed at this stage of the proceedings, the Defence cannot challenge that. The probative value, mutual contradiction, or failure of a witness statement to convince will be the subject of a special analysis and will be the subject of the Defence case. At this point in time, however, this form of de facto responsibility on the part of Mr. Sljivancanin is not something that we ask the Chamber to assess. Based on all of the above, the Defence seeks that this Honourable Chamber acquit the accused Sljivancanin on all counts of the indictment, Counts 1 to 8, described as part of a joint criminal enterprise or any other form of criminal responsibility under Article 7(1) of the Statute. We seek that the Chamber acquit our client on all counts, Counts 1 to 8, of the indictment in relation to his de jure command responsibility. I thank you for your attention, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. As previously indicated, we will now break until 1.45, which is the normal time to resume after lunch, and then hear the Prosecution for an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Before I commence my submission, may I just reply very briefly in respect of two or three matters. The first relates to two of my learned friends who complain about the witnesses or observe that the witnesses that we call to some extent represents an unfairness. We would submit that the Prosecution call witnesses, it's for them to decide, it is their prerogative, the criteria that we attempt to apply is, firstly, that the witnesses are believable and are inherently truthful; and, secondly, that they are endeavoring to be accurate. It does not preclude in any way at all the Defence from calling any witnesses that they deem appropriate. It is a matter for them. Secondly, most of the submissions that have been made by my learned friends seem to deal with the perception and the evaluation of the evidence itself. In our submission, unless evidence is wholly and utterly unreliable, over and above a phrase I think that this Court has actually used, that an extremely negative view of the credibility of a witness, Rule 98 bis proceedings are not the appropriate forum for such an assessment. The submissions that my learned friends have made therefore seem to have two principal planks. The first is that there was or is no common plan as alleged in respect of all of the defendants; and, secondly, with regard to Sljivancanin and Mrksic principally, and obviously Radic as well, there has not been demonstrated command and control in respect of the evacuation. May I just indicate to assist the Court that I will deal with Mrksic and Sljivancanin, and my learned friend Mr. Smith will deal with Radic, and Mr. Weiner will deal with the preliminary matter of wide-spread and systematic -- the evidence of wide-spread and systematic criteria. The Prosecution case itself is based on clearly circumstantial evidence against all three defendants. There are instances when one can see specific evidence and direct evidence, and therefore I intend to reply individually, if I may, but try to interlink some of the evidence that relates both to Mrksic and Sljivancanin in particular. Dealing with the preliminary points, in respect of Mrksic, his position and de jure powers, clearly, and I think it is accepted, that Mrksic was the commander of the Guards Motorised Brigade from July 1990 until the 30th of June, 1992. And he took over command of the JNA Operational Group South on the 8th of October. And there has evidence -- been evidence of that, Exhibit 401, and the evidence of Trifunovic. He commanded over OG South. That ended on the 24th of November. And as far as we're aware, the last available order signed by Mrksic as a commander of OG South is dated the 23rd of November, that is Exhibit, as I say, 426. The zone of responsibility of OG South covered an area of about eight kilometres wide, about 14 kilometres long, which in the wider area of Vukovar and described by Trifunovic, he particularised the boundaries themselves, and I won't go into that. But we would submit that as commander of operations or as commander of Operations Group South, Mrksic had importantly the exclusive right to issue orders, to command all units that included -- were included in OG South and bore full responsibility as stated in the principles of the 1984 JNA brigade rules. And that was explained by Trifunovic and that can be found at Exhibit, I believe, 395. Again, as reflected by the two experts, Pringle and Theunens, those units who were subordinated to him included regular and reserve JNA forces, Territorial Defence units and paramilitary/volunteer units. In particular, those units included the guards brigade, the 80th Motorised Brigade, the local Serb TO and the volunteers in the Leva Supoderica. We would submit that it is significant that the documentary evidence and that of the witnesses such as Trifunovic and Theunens and Pringle demonstrate that Mrksic had, and I put in inverted commas, effective control over these nominated units until at least the 21st of November, 1991, and that was at 0600 hours. That, clearly, the Court will remember as being what I will call the resubordination order; Exhibit 422. We would submit that inferentially that demonstrates that the units that I have already mentioned were subordinated to him up until that time. In respect of what I will call the effective control of perpetrators, we would submit that Mrksic's ability to command and control the other two accused, Sljivancanin, who was chief of the security organs, and Radic, who was a company commander, is evident and, as far as I can recollect, not disputed. I seem to remember that that is agreed fact 21 in relation to that. So you have by all accounts and indeed agreed, I think, by the Defence that there was a subordination link with Mrksic, Sljivancanin and Radic. Secondly, with reference to the local Serb Vukovar TO, we would submit it's clear that Mrksic asserted control over them, that was principally an order from his superior, Adzic, and that was an order, I believe, the 12th of October, where Mrksic was ordered, and I quote, "All armed units, be they JNA, TO, or volunteer units, must act under the single command of the JNA." That is Exhibit 89. We submit that unity and singleness of command is key for the understanding of the presentation of this evidence and the way that the JCE operated. There has been, in our submission, consistent evidence that has been presented in respect of Adzic's order, the order of the 21st of November to which I've already referred, that clearly demonstrates that the local units were subordinated to Mrksic and clearly under the control of Mrksic during and after the crimes that were committed at Ovcara. There have been a number of orders in relation to that, but I will not go into the particular details of those orders. More particularly, when one looks at effective control over the local Serb TO, and I say it's evidenced by Mrksic's ability to issue the order, there is a clear indication that he nominates Miroljub Vujovic as commander of the Vukovar TO. One will find that in evidence from Trifunovic, which is T8210, T standing for transcript. This order made official a situation which, in effect, de facto had existed since October, 1991 where Vujovic had replaced the previous TO commander. And again, because of the SFRY doctrine -- well, perhaps I won't deal with that, because that will take too much time. But finally, Mrksic's effective control is also substantiated by the evidence of the control of his subordinated officer, Radic, over the TO itself. That effective control and the subordination under Radic can be found in the following witnesses: P-022, P-024, Trifunovic himself, P-002, and P-018. Contrary to what has been submitted by my learned friend, we submit that there is strong evidence that Radic was in effective control of these units to which were subordinated to him. Thirdly, and with reference to the Leva Supoderica, that detachment was led by Lancuzanin, known as Kameni, and again, Mrksic's effective control over these volunteers, prior, during and after the offences at Ovcara, is evidenced in two respects. Firstly by what we will call consistent or supporting testimony of the witnesses such as Trifunovic, P-022, P-024, P-018, and additionally, P-001. And then secondly, by the orders and reports which were issued by Mrksic as commander of OG South. As I say, many of those orders continued right up until -- the implementation of those orders continued right up until the time that they left Vukovar. We submit that one of the most probative elements or aspects of the evidence of his control over the Leva Supoderica can be seen from that the unit was, in fact, subordinated to Mrksic's subordinate, and secondly -- and that being Radic, and secondly that Radic admitted to this when he was interviewed about the conflict by a journalist and answered to the question: "Who were your soldiers?" Answer: "At one point there were about 500 people of different nationalities with different party affiliations in the company which I commanded. There were active servicemen, volunteers, reservists, Chetniks and Serbian volunteers. I had to unite them under one command to ensure success. And this was achieved with hard work at all times of the day." That quotation can be found in relation to Exhibit 353. Therefore, we would submit, in conclusion in relation to that topic, that there is evidence that Mrksic had effective control over the units who were responsible for the murders at Ovcara on the night of the 20th. May I deal with, I think, the submission of the Defence in respect of his participation and knowledge. As I've already submitted, Mrksic clearly held a position of authority over those who committed the crimes, although clearly there is no evidence of him directly ordering the crimes. We accept that. That is perfectly true. What we submit is that when one looks at the circumstantial evidence that exists in this case, that his behaviour drives one to the inescapable conclusion that his clear intention was the persecution of the evacuees from the hospital itself. We would submit that Mrksic himself demonstrated, my words, a ruthless disregard for the fate of the prisoners, and we rely on the following: That there is not one significant piece of evidence that demonstrates his concern for these evacuees, nor is there any order issued by him directly reflecting the fears and concerns of his superior Zivota Panic. And we would submit that that is a very cogent piece of evidence. It is the omission that we would submit drives one to certain conclusions. In the context of the joint criminal enterprise, Mrksic's behaviour was such that it would be a logical inference that he intended the persecution. There was clearly a large amount of inaction by him, despite the notice which he received in various forms from various individuals, and, as I say, demonstrating that he did not care at the very least, and we would submit supports the allegation of his direct and intentional involvement. May I just deal with what I will call the six heads of notice, and I will refer to them in due course as well. Firstly, we know from Pringle that the general situation was tense, that there had been fighting of a form that would clearly cause concern to any observant commander. Secondly, there was the notice from Zivota Panic, Exhibit 415, which we would submit, using good old-fashioned English, demonstrated as plain as a pikestaff that there was significant concerns, not only that behaviour would occur, or bad behaviour would occur, that behaviour had already occurred with subordinated local units. It is the fact that it is not just a fear. We submit that in actual fact Zivota Panic's document shows quite clearly that it had already occurred in other areas. Thirdly, and I accept that there are evidential constraints in relation to this, but Vujic gave evidence and said that Tomic had spoken to Mrksic on the 20th about the behaviour, I believe, at the JNA barracks. I understand the evidential constraints in relation to Tomic; however, it is there in the form of Vujic's account. Fourthly, Vujic himself gave very specific evidence about the notice at what had been occurring at Velepromet. And the Court will have in mind, and I perhaps don't need to repeat what was said, but if he is to be believed, and that's a matter for the Court, then it is perfectly plain that the notice that was given to Mrksic preceded in time, namely the 19th, a situation where that which Panic had feared was actually occurring within his own zone of responsibility, and as such he was under a duty to react immediately. Fifthly, we have got Vojnovic who gives evidence that on the 20th, as a direct consequence of his accidental visiting Ovcara and what was occurring, he had attended a briefing that evening or early afternoon, if that is a contentious point, but clearly he put Mrksic on notice in respect of that. And then sixthly, that Vukosavljevic also -- who was the security organ of the 80th, also attend slightly after Vojnovic had spoken to Mrksic and he himself had indicated to Mrksic his particular concerns. What is perfectly clear is that Mrksic did nothing. The phrase I think that was used by Vojnovic was that Mrksic did not want to be bothered with these sort of things. What can be submitted of course, but here we are at 98 bis submissions, what can be submitted is, well, this is perfectly capable of demonstrating a failure to prevent under the 7(3) obligation. But in our submission one has to look at the totality of the evidence itself. Because there is a continuous and repetitive theme and it demonstrates quite clearly that Mrksic himself did absolutely nothing. And the Court is perfectly entitled, perhaps not at this juncture, to say why not. Mrksic was clearly responsible for carrying out the evacuation. It has been submitted that he was unaware about the evacuation itself. In our submission, that is not correct. There is clear evidence, not only from Bosanac, but also two other areas, and hopefully I will locate them in a moment, that demonstrate that Mrksic was aware that an evacuation was to occur. That was a private conversation with Bosanac on the 19th of November. Also, of course, there is documents from his superiors indicating quite clearly that he had responsibility for the hospital itself. The order that Mrksic issued on the morning of the 20th instructed his subordinates to, and I quote, "Evacuate and transport civilians, the wounded and the sick from the hospital in Vukovar." Again, we would submit, bearing in mind the publicity and the circumstances at that time, it was perfectly obvious that an evacuation was to occur and that in actual fact he was aware of the obligations imposed upon him by what has been called often the Zagreb agreement. The fact that Mrksic put Sljivancanin in charge of the evacuation does not remove his military and personal responsibility. Theunens, in his evidence, stated that a commander can delegate some of his powers, but he still remains responsible for the work of the officers to whom he transfers some of his rights. And we would equally submit that Pringle was actually firmer in relation to that topic, that the obligation and duty which is imposed upon Mrksic as a superior commander is ongoing. And to some extent it reinforces the old adage that one can waive a right but one cannot waive a duty, and Mrksic had a duty in relation to this evacuation and other matters. Again, Mrksic was quite aware of the existence and contents of the evacuation. The evidence of Trifunovic is firm on that. Trifunovic stated on the 19th, in the evening, it was agreed with Dr. Bosanac to carry out the evacuation of the hospital. And there is again, we would submit, matters in relation to that. So when one looks at the chronology of the events, Mrksic knew, and he had reasons to know that troops subordinated to him had not only the propensity but later on certainly were committing violent and wicked acts. And that quite simply, they were committed by units that were directly subordinated to him. May I just deal with the situation that was prevailing in his zone of responsibility, because again there seems to be a submission in respect of that. We would submit that Mrksic was well aware of the situation that was prevailing in his zone of responsibility. If I just digress, Pringle himself indicated that a commander has a double duty. He has a duty to ensure that within his zone of responsibility he is aware of what is occurring, and of course there is an obligation to ensure that all matters are reported to him. That is the purpose of singularity or unity of command. Trifunovic testified that problems were reported on all three days, meaning the 18th, 19th, and the 20th, indicating that verbal abuse, physical assaults by local population and TO members were occurring. And again, Trifunovic indicates that Mrksic was aware of these problems. He was told about them, and he was told about the problems by commanders of his subordinate units and also by the Chief of Staff as well as the head of security. One obviously bears in mind that the Chief of Staff, there is two pieces of evidence to demonstrate that Panic was actually at Ovcara; one, there is evidence from a witness who was nearby, and I will come to that in a moment; and secondly, there was evidence that Panic had spoken to Vojnovic in conversation and indicated that he was actually there. Again, in relation to what was to occur for the joint criminal enterprise, one of the most important pieces of evidence is the evidence of 017. Because on the afternoon of the 20th the contentious time is somewhere between 2.30 and 3.30, and the time is important, that 017 gave evidence that a JNA soldier, he was described as neat and clean-shaven, requested that a hole had to be dug in the proximity of Ovcara. Dimensions were given, and the person who drove the vehicle remembered seeing four or five buses outside the Ovcara hangar at the relevant time. He said that he saw the civilians being unloaded, and by the time he returned there was only a group of soldiers outside the hangar itself. We submit that the timing is crucial, because it coincides with the arrival of the buses, and we would submit it clearly demonstrates an intention to kill. Because there is no other purpose for a hole to be dug in respect of that dimension. And if memory serves me correctly, the number of bodies that were actually found in that grave were 198, and when one looks at the operations log, I think of the 80th Motorised Brigade, I think it's 1800 hours on the 19th, there is reference, I believe, to 200 people to be expected to be taken from the hospital. In any event, we would submit that that is a very important piece of evidence because the description itself tends not to suggest either a TO or irregular person. As I've already indicated, on the evening of the 20th Vojnovic and Vukosavljevic spoke to Mrksic about what they had seen had occurred. Again, dealing with what I will call notice, but also demonstrating direct control by Mrksic, there was evidence that Captain Vezmarovic, who was the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade's military police company had, of course, been placed at Ovcara and he was subsequently removed. We would submit that his evidence really strikes not only at Mrksic, but also at Sljivancanin, because quite clearly here the person who informed him is Karanfilov, who was security organ and directly subordinated to Mrksic/Sljivancanin, and also the presence of the other officer, namely Vukasinovic. And Vukasinovic himself was also directly linked to Sljivancanin. He was his immediate subordinate. So we would submit that there is very clear and cogent evidence that two senior officers who were directly subordinated to both Mrksic and Sljivancanin were present at Ovcara not only when people were being attacked, but also, and we would submit this again is an important piece of evidence, in relation to witness 001, who we would submit arrived after the military police company had departed. And it was there that he met Vukasinovic and stayed for 10 or 15 minutes and then was told to leave. It is accepted, of course, that he said that it was possible that it was the 18th, but we know the 18th was the Mitnica evacuation without problem. We would submit there is clear evidence it was the 20th, and as such he is probably the last witness in the chain of time demonstrating that both Vukasinovic and Karanfilov were both there. And, again, at that time he describes seeing terrified expressions on the faces of people and the proximity of gun-fire, although it is quite clear and it is accepted by the Prosecution he could not say definitively where it was coming from, although I seem to remember he said approximately 500 metres. Again, dealing with one of the complaints of my learned friend, on the 21st of November, the grave digger returned to his place of work, and he was told on that occasion that it would not be necessary to fill in the hole because that had already been done. Complaint is made that in actual fact there is no such reference to bulldozers. We would submit that there is reference to that. And there is also reference to 001 who indicated that he had a conversation with another officer from the JNA who had indicated that the graves had been covered at Ovcara throughout that period by a bulldozer. Again, if I may just briefly deal with it, because of, as I say, time constraints, the failure to prevent and punish crimes. We submit that from Pringle, from Theunens, from Trifunovic, and from others that there was clearly a well-defined functioning command and control system with information orders flowing up and down the chain of command and is also something that the Court may take into account. This is no average regiment. This is the elite of the elite, where discipline is paramount. And in respect of that, we would submit that there clearly demonstrate -- or is demonstrated that there is not a single piece of evidence demonstrating that measures were taken either to prevent the crimes or to punish the perpetrators and that there were no measures taken to punish those perpetrators that were subordinated to. We rely on 022 and Trifunovic in respect of that. May I move to Sljivancanin, although they don't necessarily break into two component parts, and there is much overlap and I apologise for that. But may I deal, please, with his position and de jure part. Again, he was appointed chief of the security organ on the 12th of August, 1991, and he stayed in that position until the 2nd of September, 1992. As of -- Mrksic remained commander, as I say, of the Guards Motorised Brigade until the 30th of June, 1992.
