Consequently, again, we submit that Sljivancanin was subordinated to Mrksic from the 12th of August, 1991 until September 1993. And furthermore, Sljivancanin was subordinated to Mrksic under different functions. That you will find, I think, in relation to admission 21. Sljivancanin himself, his function as chief of the security organ consisted of counter-intelligence work, the provision of expert management to the military police units, and expert advice to the commander in the use of military police. In terms of legal powers, it's, I think, common ground that the security organ had no de jure command responsibility under the regulations. However, we would submit that it was always within the power of Mrksic to order Sljivancanin in relation to various tasks. And we again submit that there has been evidence presented before the Court that show that Sljivancanin acted far and wide beyond the scope of a security officer, and we submit that it implies the existence of command responsibility. Furthermore, as of the 19th of November there is evidence that shows that Mrksic and Veselin Sljivancanin with de jure command responsibility over all the members of the forces that participated in the OG-led evacuation, respective detention of individuals, that were taken from the Vukovar Hospital and unfortunately murdered on the night of the 20th and early morning of the 21st. Therefore, we would submit that there are two issues that have to be determined. Firstly, can command responsibility be delegated to a subordinate such as Sljivancanin; and secondly, did Mrksic delegate or vest these powers in Sljivancanin. May I deal, please, with the first matter, whether in actual fact powers relating to command and control can be delegated. We submit that there has been extensive evidence on this point. We submit that the security officers can indeed exercise command responsibility prerogatives like any other JNA officer. There has been evidence presented of the security organs giving assignments to members of the Guards Motorised Brigade other than security officers, I rely on 001 in relation to that, or the possibility of being empowered with the authority of commanding officers by the commanding officers themselves. We submit the security officers can perform documents beyond their prescribed roles by being put in charge of different military activities or even command positions. For example, we know that Vukasinovic, who was subordinated to Sljivancanin, was appointed commander of the town of Negoslavci on the 9th of November. And that was based on an order of Mrksic. Again, Trifunovic, who was the author of the diary, confirmed that Mrksic had the ability to vest command powers in Vukasinovic and -- as a result of the order that Mrksic had issued. Therefore, as a former Guards Motorised Brigade officers had confirmed, security organs, although JNA regulations, they did not have de jure responsibility, could be empowered with that. And we would again suggest that the Prosecution submits here that what indeed happened, by example with regard to Vukasinovic, happened on the 19th, 20th of November, when Mrksic put Sljivancanin in charge of the evacuation of the Vukovar Hospital. As to the second issue which has to be addressed, and that is whether Mrksic, in fact, did delegate these powers, we submit that in actual fact that Vujic himself in his evidence indicated that that had actually occurred. That Sljivancanin had the responsibility for the evacuation generally, which, of course, included the hospital. Numerous witnesses, patients and people staying at the hospital also confirm, we would submit, the exercise of the delegation of those powers. I refer to them as crime-base witnesses, and I'm not going to go into them, if I may. But there is a large block of evidence which suggest that Sljivancanin was behaving in a way that left no one in any doubt at all, and we would submit it was his clear intention to so do, that he was responsible for that evacuation. Again, expert witnesses have submitted that Sljivancanin appeared to play a greater command role by being in charge of the organisation and the conducting of the evacuation at the hospital further than one would have expected from an officer in his appointment. Again, when one looks at the order, it is extremely vague, which we would submit it's indicated that the drafting of such orders in the way that it was done is highly unusual. Clearly Pringle indicated that it was of a delicate and high-profile nature, and an evacuation operation like the one in the Vukovar Hospital would normally require very detailed and specific written orders. That clearly is not the case. Pringle said that the commander is fully responsibility for everything that happens under his command, and by those under his command in his area of responsibility. And finally, with regard to Sljivancanin, he says that absolute authority and absolute responsibility to carry out the order assigned to him in the manner ascribed by his commander, who we say is obviously Mrksic, that remains responsible and accountable to his commander for the proper conduct of the task. So we would submit that there is clear evidence, not only from the experts, but also from the crime-base witnesses that Sljivancanin had de facto control. And if I try and read between the lines of my learned friend, Mr. Lukic, that does seem to be that he accepts that. Perhaps I'm wrong. If not, we submit it in any event. With regard to the effective control over the perpetrators, we would submit that there is again large amounts of evidence that demonstrate that Sljivancanin did have control over them. That he not only had de facto, he had de jure command and control over those perpetrators who committed the crimes at Ovcara and also at the Vukovar Hospital and that he exercised the prerogatives that were given to him. On the 20th of November, Sljivancanin had two encounters with the representative Borsinger. The Court have heard that. But it's perfectly clear that Sljivancanin was dealing, or was behaving in a way that demonstrated quite clearly that he was de facto in charge. Furthermore, Sljivancanin prevented the representatives of the ICRC and the ECMM from visiting the Vukovar Hospital in the early hours of the 20th. And indeed there is suggestions and the document from the ICRC -- no, the ECMM on the 19th that there was a blocking of Sljivancanin getting to the hospital -- I beg your pardon, a blocking of the ICRC getting to the hospital on the 19th. Secondly, we have presented evidence that in the early afternoon, once the selection and first evacuation had taken place, that the media was finally gained access to the hospital compound, and there there was an argument. Clearly there was a suggestion that Sljivancanin had breached the agreement. And so we would submit that Sljivancanin, in all probability, wanted to avoid the Mitnica surrender, which had been conducted under the presence of the international observers and fully covered by the media. Again, when one looks at his behaviour at the hospital on the 20th, one can see that Sljivancanin is accompanied by regular JNA soldiers, reservists, members of the local TO, when he called the hospital staff. Again, there is a selection process, and Captain Radic is clearly involved in that. What we would submit is there are two particular parts. One, the lie that Sljivancanin told to the witness when she asked what was happening to the men, that he said that they were merely going to go to the JNA barracks to be interviewed and then they would join the ladies on their way, I think to Sremska Mitrovica. That was clearly a lie, there was never any interviews at the JNA barracks, and it was a way for Sljivancanin to placate persons who may have created problems for him. Secondly, in relation to the hospital, and perhaps one of the most important pieces of evidence in the case, we would submit, is what I will call the reselection process which occurred when individuals who had been evacuated to the JNA barracks had been taken out of the buses and sent back to the hospital. When they were brought back to the hospital, there was a second screening process. And that occurred when Sljivancanin was assisted by members of the local Serb TO, that was Bogdan Kuzmic, and Miroljub Vujovic. We would submit this demonstrates a clear collusion by Sljivancanin where he was using individuals who clearly should not have been involved in any innocent activity. Because that, of course, is what has been suggested. But there has been evidence about Kuzmic's attitudes, we already know about Miroljub Vujovic, and clearly this is evidence of Sljivancanin operating hand in hand with the local TO. The reference for selection was whether they were ideologically suitable, or Ustasha. And approximately five or six people were put back on the bus, apparently due to their alleged political affiliation as a consequence of the discussion and advice given by Kuzmic and Miroljub, and the bodies of those people who were put back on the bus were also found and unfortunately exhumed in Ovcara. The double, and in actual fact it is the treble selection process. Firstly, at the hospital; secondly, at the JNA barracks, where the buses were used as nothing more than mobile prisons with TO behaving outside in an appalling and intimidating way; and then, thirdly, the reselection process clearly demonstrates that there is a policy to deal with certain individuals. Here there is also the assistance of Radic and as I say the local Serb TO, and we would submit it indicates or demonstrates the required mens rea or intent for the crimes charged. Indeed, it also puts into evidence the wide-spread and systematic targeting of civilian population of Croat and non-Serb ethnicity consistent during all the attack, this time at the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We would submit that Sljivancanin had not the authority to select the alleged defenders. There is evidence from Trifunovic that under the regulations that, and I quote, "The establishment of the identity or status of captured members of enemy armed forces is in the competence in specially designated military authorities." As I say, it demonstrates his use of the local TO with local knowledge, it demonstrates his closeness to the local TO performing the task of selection, and reinforces the Prosecution argument that he was in command and control of the evacuation. We would submit, and I will try and abbreviate as best I can, that, again, at the JNA barracks Sljivancanin was seen there holding a heated argument with Vujanovic and Vojnovic. And indeed we would submit that 009, the witness that we would reply upon on that, we would also submit that it's actually logical for Sljivancanin to be present, because if he is in charge of the evacuation it has a beginning and presumably an end. Again, at Ovcara there is evidence that Sljivancanin was there. We again rely on -- may I just check my reference, one moment, please. Yes. There is evidence that he was there. That is the witness Zlogledja. And there is also evidence that he could have clearly issued an order that he witnessed the beatings and did nothing to prevent them. From memory, there are two people who saw him at Ovcara. I've already dealt with Vukasinovic, and I've already dealt with Karanfilov. With regard to corroborating evidence, there was a military witness who was told -- 001 was told by another JNA officer who apparently had been present at Ovcara that Mrksic and Sljivancanin had ordered the killings and Sljivancanin and Radic organised the evacuation. Can I try and abbreviate it in this way, that the responsibility vested in [sic] Mrksic on Sljivancanin with regard to the evacuation was consistent with the role that Sljivancanin adopted. And again, to try and demonstrate examples of effective control, there is evidence on the 19th of November, when Okun and Vance arrived, that Sljivancanin was there acting in a role that led everyone to believe that he was in charge. I don't seek to rely upon, for this purpose, the fact that Sljivancanin apparently drew his rifle against Vance, but clearly there is evidence that he is acting in that way. In the afternoon of the 19th, Sljivancanin was in charge of the first evacuation from Vukovar Hospital to Velepromet. Again, according to numerous witnesses, P-007 and Bosanac. Again, there was another argument with the ICRC representative which I have already referred to. He was present in Negoslavci, together with the ICR representative Borsinger when he showed the ECMM representatives around, making sure that they would not gain access to the hospital. And so we would submit that there is a large amount of evidence to demonstrate that he had de facto control actually over a period of time. From the 12th until the 18th of November, again there is evidence principally from 002 that Sljivancanin was the person who was involved and giving the impression of being in charge. He was the person to be contacted by a foreign journalist if he wished to be granted permission to shoot film in the principality itself, or in the municipality, sorry. That is from Van Lynden. Sljivancanin assigned the journalist a unit headed by 001. Again, Sljivancanin was engaged in monitoring the situation and inspection of what was going on. Trifunovic gives very clear evidence about that, where he says, quite simply, provided an insight into the status and degree of accomplishment of the assigned task. That relates to the war diary. And so there is an inference that if he is inspecting, and quite simply that is one of the principal hallmarks of command and control, and Pringle also referred to that. And then there is evidence about him correcting fire. And finally, there is reference to Sljivancanin introducing to Vojnovic members of the local TO and saying that they were important people in the Territorial Defence. I will exclude, and I'm sorry if I'm running over my time. I will try and deal with it very quickly. With regard to his participation and knowledge, he was on notice about the local Serb TO. He was well aware of the undisciplined nature of the units themselves. Again, I have already referred to his control at the hospital. Again, when it came to the Velepromet facility, Sljivancanin had indicated that it was within the zone of responsibility of OG South, and one will not forget what Vujic had said, but that when he was on his way to Velepromet, that Sljivancanin had uttered the words, "Don't be surprised if you see Chetniks slaughtering Ustasha." We would submit at 98 bis proceedings that is an important piece of evidence demonstrating a clear agreement with a course of conduct to parties who were subordinated to OG South. When Vujic informed him what was happening at Velepromet, Sljivancanin's reaction was basically nothing except the words "mission completed." In respect of other matters, Radic, as I say, Mr. Smith will deal with that. Witness Trifunovic said that Sljivancanin, he was always, practically every day -- yes, he was always, practically every day at the front lines of contact with the enemy as a senior officer and security organ senior officer, that was not his duty. And he was often at Stanko Vujanovic's house, which was considered to be one of the local Serb TO command posts. We rely on P-002, P-018 in relation to that evidence. And we would submit that there was clear interaction by the local TO, and he had the opportunity of being informed of the different reports and orders. So again, we would submit that there is clear evidence in relation to Sljivancanin and Mrksic's involvement in respect of the allegations that arise in the indictment. Your Honour, I have run slightly over time. I apologise for that. May Mr. Smith now deal with the case against Radic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Your Honours, I'm making a brief response in relation to the motion put forward by the Radic defence. First, the first point is that the Prosecution, as my learned friend has just stated, is that the standard that was put forward by Mr. Borovic in relation to the 98 bis, that -- namely that the credibility of witnesses and inconsistencies or contradictions between the evidence of Prosecution witness is more appropriately addressed at the closing of the case. And as my learned friend has also put forward, if it is the case that a witness's evidence is to be rejected by the Trial Chamber, it really needs to be at a level that is really incapable -- incapable of belief or so unconvincing that no jury could convict on it. Having that in mind, Your Honour, I would submit that the witnesses that have given evidence in relation to Mr. Radic certainly do not fall within that standard. And moreover, I would submit that the way that the evidence should be looked at at this stage should be in its totality rather than in isolation. As we can see in the case of Radic, there is a number of areas in relation to his effective control over the units at Ovcara and in relation to his knowledge of the likelihood that his units would commit crimes at Ovcara, evidence in relation to his participation in the evacuation and the transfer of prisoners to Ovcara, where they were ultimately killed, and evidence in relation to his knowledge as to what, in fact, happened at Ovcara after -- after the event is corroborated by a number of the Prosecution witnesses. And as a starting point, I would ask that that be borne in mind by the Trial Chamber. Your Honours, before I commence highlighting and perhaps illustrating some of the main evidentiary points that would support a dismissal of the motion by the Defence Radic, I would just like to make a brief remark about the crime-base evidence itself. Mr. Radic's [sic] motion isn't largely based on the underlying crimes but on his client's participation in them. But in relation to the underlying crimes, I think it was put forward by Mr. Domazet, that we -- the Prosecution has only provided solid evidence in relation to 200 victims being killed at Ovcara, not 264 as outlined in the indictment. That is -- that is correct in the sense that 200 bodies were found at Ovcara. As Your Honours would be aware from the evidence of Dr. Strinovic and Mr. Grujic, that 190 of those bodies had been identified and are contained in the Annex A to the indictment. There were two further identified that were identified after the indictment was issued, and eight are still remaining to be identified. In effect, that leaves 74 people in Annex A that haven't been identified as being killed at Ovcara. In relation to that, Your Honour, I would like to put forward the fact that when witnesses testified at the trial, a number of witnesses stated that of those 74 at least 11, or the totality of their evidence is that at least 11 of those witnesses -- 11 of those victims were either identified at Ovcara in the hangar or, alternatively, on the bus, or on one of the buses that left Vukovar Hospital and subsequently ended up at Ovcara. And if I can briefly state their names. The victims that there has been evidence to establish -- that evidence has established that are: Ante Bodrozic, Zorislav Gaspar, Milan Grejza, Damir Kovacic, Drago Krizan, Josip Mikletic, Ceman Saiti, Damjan Samardzic, Zvonko Vulic, Viktor Horvat and Karlo Fitus. So, Your Honours, the Prosecution would like Your Honours to take that into account in deciding whether or not there has been enough evidence to support the fact that those men were killed at Ovcara, and it's the Prosecution's submission that there is enough in relation to the 98 bis standard. As far as the other 70 -- the remaining of the 74 that haven't been identified at Ovcara, neither in the grave or by other witnesses, the Prosecution would like the Court to note that a number of those people were identified as missing from the Vukovar Hospital on the 20th of November in the missing person's reports. And -- and as well a number of the victims, at least 16, as Your Honours have heard, have been found in other graves. But in relation to the 190 plus the 11 victims that I have mentioned, I would submit that the Prosecution has proved to the appropriate standard that those people were killed at Ovcara. Your Honour, if I can now turn to a submission in relation to Radic's responsibility under Article 7(1) and 7(3). I will reduce the evidence that forms the core basis of his liability to some core evidentiary topics, and in doing so I hope I address the questions raised, or the doubts raised by my learned friend, the topics being evidence of Radic's effective control over the perpetrators, his participation in the evacuation and transfer of the detainees that were killed at Ovcara, his knowledge or other knowledge of the likelihood that these crimes would be committed by his subordinates, and his knowledge that these crimes in fact were committed by his subordinates and his failure to prevent and punish the perpetrators. Having established an evidentiary basis for these core issues, it is our submission if Your Honour accepts that that evidence has been placed before you, that both theories of liability under Article 7(1) and 7(3) are substantiated. In relation to Radic's effective control over the perpetrators that beat and killed the Croats and non-Serbs at Ovcara, the best evidence in relation to his effective control is, in fact, what's been mentioned by my learned friend, Mr. Radic's own admission to a journalist, Mr. Kacarevic, that spoke to him four days after the killings. In that magazine he stated that he commanded up to 500 men, and then he stated after he reorganised the troops he then managed or commanded a unit of up to 300 men. This statement was unchallenged by the Defence, and perhaps provides the most probative evidence as to what Mr. Radic's role was in Vukovar. Also, in that article Mr. Radic responded to a question, "What exactly happened when Vukovar fell?" He stated that he reorganised from 500 to 300 and then they were able to take street by street, block by block more effectively ground in Vukovar, and that's how it fell. So in my submission, even on that statement alone by Mr. Radic, it can be inferred that on his -- on his own words, that he commanded the Leva Supoderica unit, the TO volunteers, and the guards brigade company right up until the Vukovar -- Vukovar fell, on his own words. As far as who the perpetrators of Ovcara were, it's -- that evidence was provided by P-022. He clearly stated that the commanders of the Leva Supoderica unit, the commander of Miroljub Vujovic's unit, which -- being Miroljub Vujovic, Milan Lancuzanin and about 16 or 17 others, most of which by the tendering of the judgement today can be seen to have been convicted at the Belgrade court for the killing of these people. The people that committed the crimes at Ovcara weren't just any members of Radic's unit, they were the commanders of -- of the units that he commanded. And in terms of knowledge as to -- Radic's knowledge as to the killings, that is an important detail. As far as the accused's effective control over the assault group or unit that he commanded which he states in his interview, this is supported by other witnesses. It is supported by P-022, (redacted) (redacted). It is also supported by P-018, another member of his company. It's also supported by P-024, a member of the Leva Supoderica unit that was fighting in Vukovar. The effective control can be seen -- or the extent of his control can be seen when P-024 was asked who was the commander of your unit, the Leva Supoderica unit, and he replied it's Mr. Radic. Whether that's true or not, and, in fact, it appears to be the evidence that it was the person called Kameni, it certainly indicates the close proximity that Mr. Radic had to these paramilitary and TO units. Each of these witnesses provided independent testimony which arrives generally at the same conclusion. But as to the duration of the effect of the control, viewed in its totality, it is submitted that the reasonable inference can be drawn from these witnesses that they view that Radic had effective control over -- over the perpetrators at Ovcara up until the event occurred and shortly beyond. In support of this, Trifunovic, as senior guards brigade officer, provided testimony that he believed that assault detachments were still in existence in Operational Group South on the 21st of November, 1991. Now, this was based on an order removing the Leva Supoderica from the 1st Battalion, or from the 1st Assault Detachment. Moreover, he stated that he believed the Assault Detachment 1 was responsible for the takeover of the hospital along with the military police battalion. The evidence is generally clear that Radic was the assault group or platoon commander in Assault Detachment 1. Supporting this contention, the Prosecution has presented witnesses who, in fact, show that Radic participated in the evacuation and transfer at the hospital of non-Serbs to Ovcara with other paramilitaries. Corroborating the fact that Radic had effective control over the assault group or platoon, which he states, including the volunteers and the TO, Theunens, a military expert at the Tribunal, testified that at the fall of -- the fall of Vukovar did not mean an end to the war, and there would still be resistance pockets, as well as a serious risk of revenge and retribution by members of the victorious forces. He stated that as a result it would be illogical that assault groups would be disbanded because command and control over all forces involved, in particular volunteers and paramilitaries, had to be maintained at the lowest possible --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, please slow down for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: [Microphone override] -- groups and assault detachments in such an unstable situation marked by a threat of revenge by undisciplined TO forces largely consisting of volunteers and paramilitaries would have been illogical from the point of view of the former Yugoslavian armed forces doctrine. That was the opinion of the expert, and that was supported by the witnesses' contentions themselves. The Defence contention that Radic's assault group ceased to exist from the 14th of November by virtue of the combat orders of the 14th and 18th of November - that's Exhibit 430 and 431 - to Tesic, does not -- because assault groups were not referred to in that order, it is submitted that that inference is not the only inference that can be drawn from those orders. Now, this can be reasonably inferred from re-examination of Trifunovic, when he stated that it was prerogative of the battalion commander to form assault groups and organise them as he sees fit and not the brigade --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Smith please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And not the brigade commander. Contrary to the Defence contention, the body of Prosecution evidence supports that Radic was still in effective control of the perpetrators on and after the 20th of November. Having such de jure and de facto powers over these perpetrators at Ovcara by formation of the assault groups within Vukovar in no way mitigates Radic's responsibility to prevent and punish crimes because, as the Defence puts it, he was a small-time commander or a mere commander, as he puts it. In Vukovar, it's clear from the accused's own statement and from his reputation in the battle-field Radic had a large command role which brought with it all the responsibilities of command and control that were testified to by Trifunovic, Theunens and Pringle. In short, there is evidence which establishes the effective control over the volunteers, TO and guards brigades, involved in the killing and beating at Ovcara and Vukovar barracks, but most importantly, Radic's own admissions, his actions in the field, the fact that he lived at the TO and volunteer headquarters, the fact that he ordered the volunteers and TO, the fact that on occasions he punished them, he removed members of the Leva Supoderica unit, the evidence in totality is established by many sources, some being P-022, P-024, P-018, P-002, P-030, Dr. Njavro, and the military experts. As to the evidence as to whether Mr. Radic participated in the evacuation and transfer of detainees or residents at the hospital, a number of witnesses testified to this fact. The evidence establishes that Radic personally participated in the takeover of the Vukovar Hospital on the 18th, 19th and then the 20th of November, 1991. The selection and transfer to Ovcara farm of the primarily non-Serb male patients or combatants who had laid down their arms where they were cruelly treated and executed. Radic's involvement in the evacuation came at an early stage, when he was present at the Vukovar Hospital on the 18th, and then the 19th, and then the 20th, with other JNA soldiers and paramilitaries. Your Honours heard the testimony of Dr. Njavro, a medical practitioner, who testified that at certain points over this three-day period, Radic, with paramilitaries, inspected, selected, detained, abused, and mistreated people staying at the hospital. He testified that the patients stated that they were abused and mistreated by Radic and a person called Bogdan Kuzmic, and told by them that they would meet their end because they knew what they had done in Vukovar. He testified that Radic told him that the mistreatment was under the orders of or with the permission of Sljivancanin. Radic's presence at the hospital is corroborated (redacted) (redacted), P-018, who states that he was at the hospital on the day that the Ovcara massacre occurred. He testified that he was with Sljivancanin, Stanko Vujanovic, another perpetrator at Ovcara, and other Chetniks. Witness -- also Witness P-030, a detainee, or a defender who had laid down their arms and sought refuge at the hospital stated that he was at the hospital on the 20th of November and he saw Sljivancanin order Radic to search prisoners that were being taken on the buses to Ovcara. Mr. Radic is not only seen at the hospital on those days, but he is also seen by witnesses at the JNA barracks, the last point before the detainees were taken to Ovcara. At the JNA barracks P-030 and another witness, P-024, a member of the Leva Supoderica unit, state that they saw Radic present with the JNA soldiers, TO and volunteers at the barracks. Witness P-030 testified that he saw him on the second occasion at the barracks, selecting people from the bus by using a list, after which some prisoners got off the bus, were beaten and taken to another bus. After the beatings P-024 further testified that -- or testified that he saw Radic in a military vehicle, a Campagnola. He saw Radic with subordinates in his unit, the head of the Leva Supoderica unit, or the commander, Milan Lancuzanin, Kameni, he saw him with Miroljub Vujovic, the commander of the TO and volunteers' unit, and he saw him with Stanko Vujanovic, commander of a TO unit, and he also saw him with Lieutenant Hadzic, a platoon commander in Radic's company. All of these men have been identified as perpetrators at Ovcara. All other than Hadzic have been identified as killers at Ovcara, and Hadzic has been identified as a beater by P-022. Radic was in the vehicle with these men that led the buses away, was in front of the buses, and the buses turned outside the Vukovar barracks away from the town and towards the direction of Ovcara with a crowd of volunteers and paramilitaries following on foot or in vehicles. That's the testimony of P-024. P-024 also testified there was an atmosphere of revenge and hatred at the barracks, and I think the other Prosecution witnesses have made that very clear, that revenge was very much something that appeared to be on the minds of the TOs and paramilitaries there. Also on that day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, you'll have to come to your conclusion quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will be brief. Also on that day, Your day, Your Honour, Your Honours heard evidence from P20 -- P-022 and P-018 that at the end of the day they told Radic what had happened at the -- at Stanko Vujanovic's house. P-022 also stated that he sent -- that Radic stated -- that Radic sent P-022 to the Ovcara -- Ovcara hangar before the crimes occurred. In relation to further knowledge as to the likelihood that the perpetrators at Ovcara would commit further crimes there, P-022, P-024, and P-018 have all presented quite significant evidence of Radic being very aware of the criminal and undisciplined behaviour of some of the members of the Leva Supoderica unit and also Miroljub Vujovic's TO unit. Further, after Radic had received knowledge that the crimes had, in fact, occurred at Ovcara, witnesses have testified, that's P-018, P-022, who were both members of the guards brigade, and also Mr. Trifunovic also testified that no investigations were conducted into any of the people that had committed the crimes by Radic. Certainly when he was in a position to do so, whilst he was in Vukovar and when he left Vukovar he was still in the position to investigate and discipline members of the guards brigade involved in those crimes such as P-022. Your Honour, on that basis I would ask that if the evidence is accepted, that those points have been established that the theories of 7(1) and 7(3) in relation to Mr. Radic are supported by that evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith. It was suggested, Mr. Weiner, that would you speak for a few minutes. I would underline "few."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The fact that you gave me a few is quite kind. Just very briefly. In passing, the issue of wide-spread and systematic was raised. The Prosecution would submit that the large-scale attack which occurred in Vukovar, the wide-scale attack which occurred through Eastern and Western Slavonia and that which occurred through Croatia satisfies the burden that a wide-spread or systematic attack occurred. As you know, in Vukovar the town was under siege, there was non-stop shelling for a period of three months from land, from water, from the air. This was an indiscriminate attack where civilian property and civilians were targeted. In fact, witness P-002 talks about a conversation he had with the people who were firing out of Borovo Selo at page 10.371, and he asked them what they were aiming at, and they indicated, "Come on, on what aiming? I just fire and wherever it lands." There were no major military targets in Vukovar. They were shelling the hospital, they were shelling the wells, they were shelling people who were going to the wells with their little tin cups. There were no tanks, there were no mortar or artillery battalions, no heavy weaponry, no fortresses to be shelled, just a number of soldiers with light weapons. This was a disproportionate attack, it was an indiscriminate attack, and the damage was unnecessary. And how do we know that it was unnecessary? Because we've heard from van [sic] Kypr who spoke to some of the soldiers, and on page 3101 of the transcript they tell him that the damage was unnecessary. They said that a professional army should not -- should have taken the city in a few days rather than a few months and destroying it completely. They mentioned that they had complained to General Kadijevic. This lengthy, sustained and excessive shelling attack on Vukovar constituted a wide-spread or systematic attack on the civilian population. Although it is not dispositive of this issue, the Pre-Trial Chamber in the review of indictment pursuant to Rule 61 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, dated 3 April 1996 discussed this issue in paragraphs 31 to 35, and at 32 they say based on the evidence which has been presented to them these events seem to be part of a wide-spread and systematic attack against the civilian population of the City of Vukovar. The Prosecution would only add that there's been a great deal of evidence relating to the wide-spread and systematic attack in Slavonia, in the ECMM reports from ECMM witnesses, from witness 002, and if you look at the extensive shelling throughout that area, the expulsions throughout that area, the expulsions throughout Croatia as discussed by Dr. Wheeler, by Mr. Grujic, and also by Ambassador Okun, who says in November there were 200.000 displaced persons, by Christmas there were 500.000 displaced persons. You can see that there was a wide-spread and systematic attack against Vukovar, both Eastern, Western Slavonia, and Baranja, and all of Croatia. The Prosecution submits that we have established that a wide-spread or systematic attack against a civilian population has occurred. Thank you for the few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber will have a break now, resuming at 10 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber is delivering its decision on the motions for acquittal by the Defence for each of the three accused in this case. Pursuant to Rule 98 bis of the Rules the Chamber is to enter, by oral decision, and after having heard oral submissions of the parties, a judgement of acquittal on any count if there is no evidence capable of supporting a conviction. The standard to be applied in respect of each count is whether, on the evidence as it stands, and taken at its highest, for the Prosecution, it would be properly open to a Trial Chamber to be persuaded beyond reasonable doubt to convict the accused. It follows that a decision that there is evidence capable of sustaining a conviction on a particular count is in no sense an indication of the view of this Chamber as to the ultimate guilt or innocence of the accused on that count. This is so, because at this stage of the case, the Chamber is not to evaluate the respective credit of witnesses or the strengths and weaknesses of contradictory or different evidence. The Chamber is required at this stage to assume that the Prosecution's evidence is, and I quote, "entitled to credence unless incapable of belief." In essence, a Rule 98 bis motion will succeed if there is no evidence supporting a particular count or if the only relevant evidence is so incapable of belief that it could not properly sustain a conviction, even when the evidence is taken at its highest for the Prosecution. I have relied there, the Chamber has, on the decisions in Jelesic of the 5th of July, 2001; Strugar of the 21st of June, 2004; and Milosevic, 16th of June, 2004. The Chamber notes that in its most recent formulation, that is since December 2004, the rule requires the Chamber to enter a judgement of acquittal when there is no evidence capable of supporting a conviction on a particular count. This is materially different from the earlier form of the rule, which turned on offences charged and a finding of the Trial Chamber. On its face, the new rule does not also require evidence capable of establishing each and every allegation, particular, or form of liability, that is criminal responsibility, pleaded in respect of a count to support a conviction on a count. There must be evidence which meets the standard that we have set out above in respect of every element of the offence alleged by the count. This may be established, even though the evidence is not necessarily sufficient in respect of some other allegations or particulars set out in the indictment in respect of that count, or in respect of one or some forms of criminal responsibility relied on by the Prosecution. The Prosecution need only ultimately succeed in proving one of the forms of criminal responsibility it relies on for there to be a conviction on a count. This approach not only accords with the rule as it is now formulated, it may also be seen to be appropriate in the particular circumstances of this case, in which the charges all arise from what is essentially one course of conduct or event. The main conduct occurred over a few hours, involving one group of detainees who were moved from the hospital via one or two locations to a farm in the Ovcara area. The trial is against three accused, each of whom were officers in the JNA engaged in the same operational area and of whom Colonel Mrksic was the overall commander. His effective command extended, at least on some evidence, beyond serving JNA personnel to include reservists, Territorial Defence personnel of various types, paramilitaries and other volunteers, including Chetniks, who were operational in that area. The Chamber therefore proposes to consider these motions on the basis of the present form of Rule 98 bis, as indicated. We will not consider, therefore, whether in respect of a count against an accused there is evidence capable of establishing all matters alleged in respect of that count, or all forms of criminal responsibility relied on. The standard which must be satisfied by the evidence adduced by the Prosecution, as we have outlined it in those comments, is the standard that we will apply throughout our consideration of the evidence. I will turn briefly to the crimes themselves that are charged in the counts. This won't be done in the order in which they appear in the indictment to avoid unnecessary repetition. Torture, Counts 5 and 7; inhumane acts, Count 6; and cruel treatment, Count 8, relate to events at the farm. The actus reus of torture is an act or omission inflicting severe mental or physical suffering of inhumane acts, an act or omission causing serious bodily harm or mental harm, or serious attack on human dignity. And in respect of cruel treatment, an act or omission causing serious physical or mental suffering or causing a serious attack on human dignity. With respect of the actus reus that are obviously closely related of those three types of offence, the Chamber has heard evidence capable of establishing that on the 20th of November, 1991, a large number of persons, some six bus loads, so between 2 and 300 persons, were transferred from the Vukovar Hospital and held for several hours at the farm in the Ovcara area, by or in the presence of Territorial Defence members, volunteers, Chetniks, military policemen, and other JNA troops. As such, the prisoners were not taking any active part in the hostilities, and the evidence shows that significant numbers of them were subjected to mistreatment. There is also evidence relating -- of a somewhat similar nature relating to events involving some of those detainees at the barracks in Vukovar. Now, I would just mention the evidence of the witnesses P-011 at pages 5728 to 34 of the transcript; Hajdar Dodaj at pages 5536 to 5540; Berghofer at 5291 to 5296; Zlogledja at 1.187 to 9; P-030 at 9745 to 47; P-014 at 7703 to 6; P-022 at pages 503, 504, 525, 5235 and 5236. The mens rea of torture is an intentional act or omission carried out with a prohibited purpose. I won't list prohibited purposes; they're settled and well-known. The mens rea of inhumane acts: Intent to cause serious harm or attack on human dignity or knowledge of probability that such harm or attack would result. And of cruel treatment: Attempt to cause suffering or attack on human dignity or knowledge of probability that such suffering or attack would result. The Chamber has heard evidence capable of establishing, first, that the mistreatments of the Ovcara farm were carried deliberately; secondly, that in some instances they were carried out for the purposes of punishment or discriminating against the victim on the basis that the victim was a Croat or a Croatian defender, or were carried out to obtain information from the victim. It did mention a variety of evidence dealing with the gauntlet, the scale of beatings, and the use of objects of various types for the purpose of beatings. And in particular, the evidence of witnesses P-014 at transcript page 7715; Berghofer at transcript 5289; P-011 at pages 5730 to 5732; P-030 at 9746 to 7; Dodaj at 5540; and P-022 at 5205 to 6, and 5236. The offences of extermination, Count 2, and murder, Counts 3 and 4, are all alleged again in the vicinity of the farm in the Ovcara area. The actus reus of extermination is an act or omission resulting in death of a person, and it's to be on a massive scale; and of murder, an act or omission resulting in death. The Chamber has heard evidence capable of establishing, first, that on the 20th of November, 1991 prisoners held at the farm were taken in groups to a nearby location where they were executed. Secondly, that a large mass grave was discovered in that locality, containing around 200 bodies. Thirdly, that for the overwhelming majority of these bodies, death was caused by gunshot, and that there were altogether a large number of prisoners at that farm. As I've mentioned before, some 200 to 300. And the witness P-002, at pages 10396 to 8; P-022, at pages 507 to 9; P-011 at 5737 to 42; P-014 at 7724 to 5; Strinovic, 9451 to 3, 9455 and Exhibit 457, 9458, Exhibit 457, and 9464 to 9465, Exhibits 459 and 60; and Milewski, Exhibit 381. Examples to the evidence which I have referred. Could it be made clear by the Chamber, that in quoting this evidence we are not suggesting that it is an exhaustive review of the evidence. We are merely using these as illustrative of the evidence that is available in support of the elements of each of the offence -- each offence charged in each count. The mens rea of extermination is an intent to cull persons on a massive scale or knowledge of the probability of deaths on a massive scale. And the mens rea of murder with intent to kill the victim or knowledge of the probability of death. The evidence is capable of establishing the deliberate nature of the executions of some 200 people. First, the modus operandi, a large number, the majority of them shot in the head, the scale of executions, the number involved, all in the one locality, buried in a mass grave, and evidence as to the expression of intention by some of the individual perpetrators. And we would just mention in respect to those two pieces of evidence, that of P-022, pages 5005 and 5006, and of Zlogledja at 1.190 to 91. Persecutions, as the offence charged in Count 1. What is required is a discriminatory act or omission infringing on a fundamental right. Much of the evidence that I have mentioned already is capable of establishing that individuals that were held at the farm at the relevant time were subjected to mistreatment and that a large number of them was executed. There must also be a discriminatory intent on one or more of the listed grounds. And the Chamber has heard evidence capable of establishing that the prisoners were mistreated and executed because they were Croats or Croatian defenders. Mention as examples the evidence of Strinovic at 9467; P-022 at 5006; Berghofer at 5289; Dodaj at 5537, 5539, and 5540; P-014 at 7715; P-030 at 9746 to 7. That, very quickly, deals with the essential elements of the offences charged and the evidence that is there. There's also a question raised in submissions by the Defence as to whether jurisdiction under Article 5 is established. That requires relevantly that there be a white-spread or systematic attack against a civilian population. Now, the evidence is capable of establishing that during the relevant period of the indictment and the closely preceding period, the town of Vukovar and its surrounding localities was under heavy shelling and that this extended over many, many weeks, in fact months, and that this led to the injury and death of a large number of civilians. There is also indication that this shelling in the Vukovar locality is also to be seen and appreciated in the context of military action in the wider Western Slavonia and indeed in the wider -- what is today Croatia. We would refer in particular to the evidence of Kolesar at 914 to 9, and 927, and also at 920 to 24, and 928 to 930. The evidence of Foro at 2402 to 3. Mr. Van Lynden at 3081, 3092, and 3146 to 49. That should be the evidence of Van Lynden at 3081 to 3092. The evidence of Agotic at 1962 and 1965 and also Exhibit P90. The evidence of Kypr at 6552 to 7, and Exhibit 312. The evidence of P-002 at 1.369 to 70, and at 1.371 and 2. The evidence of Dr. Njavro at transcript pages 1515 to 1517. The Chamber has also heard evidence capable of establishing that the acts committed at the farm were a consequential part of that attack to which I've referred and that the accused were well aware of the attack, and also establishing that the events, the subject of the counts, occurred immediately after the fall or taking of Vukovar, and that the material events involved the same troops as were involved in the taking, and that these included JNA forces, territorial forces, volunteers, and other paramilitaries. The evidence would indicate that all three accused took part in the takeover of Vukovar. The alleged victims who were civilians were also detained when the attack and -- or the takeover of Vukovar succeeded. The evidence is also capable of showing that on the 19th of 20th of November a large number of persons, which may have included some form of combatants, had laid down their weapons, were detained, were mistreated and killed by or in the presence of those various forces that I've just mentioned. I would also mention in passing evidence relating to events at Velepromet, especially the evidence of Grujic at 4514 to 4515, 42 -- 4528 to 9 and 4568, and of events at the JNA barracks in Vukovar; in particular, the witness P-009 at pages 6148 to 6151. The -- I won't repeat the evidence about the alleged particular events at the farm. There is also evidence capable of establishing that there had been an extremely large-scale displacement of the civilian population in the area, in particular the evidence of Dr. Wheeler in Exhibit 391, and evidence capable of suggesting that an attack by those forces was disproportionate to those against which they were poised. Having dealt in that general way with those general issues, I turn now to look more particularly at aspects of the evidence directed against the three accused men. In so doing, as indicated at the outset of these reasons, the Chamber will confine its attention simply to the question of the responsibility on at least one of the bases relied upon by the Prosecution as it looks at each accused. And in doing so it will look at Article 7(3) of the Statute, that is, the area of responsibility known usually as command responsibility. And it does so, as indicated, on the basis that if there is evidence capable of sustaining this, there is evidence capable of sustaining a conviction on each count. The first element of Article 7(3) is effective control. With respect to the accused Colonel Mrksic, there is evidence capable of establishing that at the relevant times Mr. Mrksic held a position of command over and the power to control the acts of some, at least, of the perpetrators. He was commander of the Guards Motorised Brigade and in time became also commander of the Operational Group South, as is an agreed fact. He was in charge in those capacities, or particularly as commander of the Operational Group South, of a zone of responsibility which included the area of Vukovar and had control operationally over the territory in which the events alleged in the indictment are alleged to have occurred. And in those respects we would refer to the evidence in particular of Dr. Bosanac, 675 to 6, and 803 to 4, and at 806; the evidence of Trifunovic at 8127; the order issued to evacuate and transport civilians, wounded and sick from the hospital on the morning of the 20th of November, 1991. The Chamber has also heard evidence capable of establishing that Mr. Mrksic had authority over the JNA, including reserve units located in that zone of operations, particularly the evidence of Bosanac at 803 to 4. Also, evidence capable of establishing that he gave assignments to JNA commanders. In particular, at Exhibit 367, which is under seal, and the evidence at pages 3 -- 7673 to 7674, the evidence of Vojnovic at pages 8849, 8680, also at 7720, and at 8169 to 73. There's also relevant evidence at 8825 to 6. And there I'm referring to evidence of witnesses Vojnovic, Vukasinovic, Trifunovic, P-014. The Chamber has also heard evidence capable of establishing that Colonel Mrksic had the command authority to issue orders to all units included in Operational Group South. This included all territorial and paramilitary units and volunteers. We refer to the evidence in particular of Trifunovic at Exhibit 395 and at transcript pages 8210, 8140; to Exhibit 424; to Exhibit 89, the communication of General Adzic of the 12th of October, 1991; also to the expert evidence of witnesses Theunens and Pringle. And this evidence is capable of showing that that command authority extended past the 20th of November, 1991. In addition to the references given, refer to Exhibit 422, an order issued by Colonel Mrksic on the 21st of November, 1991. That body of evidence, when reviewed, has the consequence that effective control by Mrksic is sufficiently demonstrated by the available evidence for the present purposes of Rule 98 bis. It must also be shown for the purposes of Article 7(3) that the accused had knowledge or reasons to know of the -- that his subordinates were about to commit criminal acts. And in respect of this, in relation to Colonel Mrksic, the evidence of Vujic at 4512 to 3, 4567 and 4706 to 7; the evidence of Trifunovic, he testified as to problems regarding security of detainees from forces under the command of Colonel Mrksic, problems that occurred on each of the 18th, 19th and 20th of November. There is also evidence that is capable of establishing the -- that the accused Colonel Mrksic was aware that his subordinates had committed criminal acts at Ovcara. In particular, the evidence of Vojnovic at 8849; witness P-014 at 7720; and Vukasinovic at 8681 to 8682. There is also the communication from Colonel Mrksic's superior, General Panic, expressing fears and concerns because of conduct of forces under Colonel Mrksic's command to that time. This is Exhibit 415. There must also be evidence capable of establishing that the accused failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent criminal acts from his subordinates. And in this respect the evidence of Vujic at 4512 to 3 and at 4567 and 4706 to 7 is perhaps a sufficient indication of that. There is also evidence capable of establishing that Colonel Mrksic failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to punish the perpetrators of the acts that are the subject of the counts. Evidence of Vojnovic and Vukasinovic at 8849 and at 8681 to 82, also at Vukasinovic at 8682; the witness Trifunovic at 8172 and 8173, the absence of any steps or orders of any type taken by Colonel Mrksic in response to General Panic's expressed concerns to which I've referred, and the witness P-022 and Trifunovic that no measures were taken to punish. Those are sufficient reviews of the evidence to indicate that in respect of command responsibility there is evidence capable of establishing the responsibility under Article 7(3) of Colonel Mrksic. Turning to the accused Captain Radic, and again looking at the evidence on the basis of Article 7(3), the issue of effective control we would refer to Exhibit 594, the agreed facts, Radic's command positions at the time. P-022, the evidence of Vujovic, and this is at 4957 to 4961 -- sorry, it's his evidence about Vujnovic, the evidence of P-022 at that page reference. Also P-022's evidence at 4955 to 60, 4965 to 72; the evidence of P-018 at 7386, 7391 to 95, and at 4979 to 4985, and at 4981 to 4985; the evidence of Kacarevic at 7292 to 3, and Exhibit 353; the evidence of P-030 concerning the conduct of Captain Radic, both at the hospital and the barracks. While this is an issue which is subject to much competing evidence, as was the case with Colonel Mrksic and is also the case with Major Sljivancanin, there is evidence relating to Captain Radic which satisfy the standard applicable to Rule 98 bis, to establish that he had effective control of units participating in the offences alleged in the counts, and that that was so at the time that the offences were committed. With respect to the requirement of knowledge, there is evidence capable of establishing that Captain Radic became aware that crimes had been committed at the farm during the night of the 20th and 21st of November. P-022 at 5009 and 5032 to 4, P-018 at 7412 to 5, P-002 at 7415 -- sorry, at 10400. With respect to the measures taken to prevent or to punish, P-022 at 5032 to 37; P-018 at 7416 to 7419; and Trifunovic at 8173. There's also evidence relating to the barracks from P-024 at pages 4202 to 6. With respect to the case against Major Sljivancanin, with respect to effective control, there is evidence capable of demonstrating that he had authority over the military police, the Guards Motorised Brigade, and the military police of other units subject to Colonel Mrksic's command as part of Operational Group South. We have the evidence of Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic at 8825, and at 8827; and of Colonel Vujic at 4533 to 4. There is also evidence capable of establishing that Major Sljivancanin had effective control over both military police and other soldiers of the JNA and of other forces at the hospital, in particular on the 20th of November. That is at least de facto control, but not intending by that comment to exclude de jure authority. If it is accepted as some evidence might well establish by way of inference that Major Sljivancanin was given special command -- a special command assignment by Colonel Mrksic, at least in respect of the evacuation of the hospital on the 20th of November, 1991, that being something that was on the evidence, on some evidence, procedurally proper and within Colonel Mrksic's powers. Now, the evidence in this regard, particularly that of Dosen at 3800 and 3803 to 5, and also at 3913 to 5. There is also some evidence capable of establishing that Major Sljivancanin had effective control over military police and other forces at Ovcara. The evidence in particular of Captain Karanfilov at 8420, 8432; the evidence of P-022 at 5020. With respect to knowledge, evidence capable of establishing that Major Sljivancanin was aware of mistreatment of detainees occurring prior to the events at Ovcara, we have the evidence of Colonel Vujic at 4525 to 6 and at 4530, and also at 4526. Evidence of capable of establishing that Major Sljivancanin was present at Ovcara at or at about the time when the alleged offences were committed, that is the evidence of Zlogledja at 10196. There's also evidence of his presence at the JNA barracks with Vujanovic and Vojnovic; see particularly the evidence of P-009. This is in the course of the movement of detainees from the hospital to Ovcara. With respect to the issue of measures to prevent, there is the evidence of Zlogledja at 10196. And with respect to failure to take measures to punish, we have Colonel Trifunovic at 8173 to 8174. Now, it will be apparent to all that there is much other evidence. There is included in that much other evidence, evidence to the contrary or evidence in contradiction of what has been referred to by the Chamber in this decision. It's not that we ignore that, we are well aware of it, but for the reasons indicated it's not evidence that we properly take into account and weigh at this time. And that is the significant difference between our role here today and the role we must perform at the close of all the evidence when we come, once again, to review not only the evidence we have mentioned today, but all the other evidence in the case. We are grateful to Judge Van Den Wyngaert, who has picked up that in the transcript at page 82, line 3, the phrase is recorded as "wide-spread and systematic attack," when I should have said, if I did not, "wide-spread or systematic attack." For the reasons that have been indicated, the Chamber is therefore of the view that there is no basis on which it can enter judgement of acquittal on any count which is set out in the indictment against any one of the three accused at the present time in its consideration of the requirements of Rule 98 bis. It is therefore the situation that the motions under Rule 98 bis, by each of the accused, will be dismissed.
